children.translated_text: pay homage to the <s>cetiya</s> (shrine). Whatever they see there that has been defiled by a dog or a jackal — whoever is the junior should clean it. But if the junior is lazy and negligent, the elder should clean it. These two monks enter the alms-round territory; naturally, first [waste] should be voided. But if a monk, having entered [the village], has the need for proper conduct — what should be done? He should go to the dwelling near the village or come to the retiring-place. It is not proper, when coming and going at a <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> (nun) residence, to enter the latrine. Many nuns may be seated there. Rather, one should ask: 'Sister, is the latrine vacant or not?' It is not proper to ask a young [nun], lest there be embarrassment. Rather, an elderly [nun] should be asked. If she says: 'Noble sir, the latrine is vacant,' taking water in a small or large water-vessel, one should enter. Having relieved oneself and washed with water, one should go. But if that too is not possible, one should go to the public privy. It is not proper to go to the women's privy. Rather, one should go to the men's privy. If there is no public privy, one should go to an abandoned house. One should ask: 'Is the cesspit vacant?' A young woman should not be asked, lest she be given cause for laughter. An older woman should be asked. If she says it is vacant, taking water-vessels, one should enter. If that too is not possible, [and] there is an empty house or a marshy place, one should go there. One should not sit at an overly exposed entry, lest one be suspected — one should sit at a concealed entry. But if that too is not possible, on an elevated road, with a wall behind, one should relieve oneself. The companion who is with him should stand in front, facing away,

children.translated_text: A monk needs to relieve himself. It is not proper to relieve oneself wherever one wishes, lest people grumble: 'By whom have entrails been scattered about here?' Rather, placing some thicket or tree behind, one should sit down. One should not do it downwind, lest the entire caravan be troubled by the smell — it should be done upwind. When the caravan has set out, the proper conduct is: one should sit to one side and do it. One should not stand up without being aware [of one's surroundings], lest one be struck [by someone thinking]: 'A thief or a robber!' One should not do it downwind, lest the caravan be troubled by the smell — it should be done upwind. It is not proper to go [about] with the lower robe merely tucked up. Rather, the lower robe should be tucked up and one should sit down. It is not proper, with the lower robe tucked up, holding the private parts with the left hand, to go hurriedly as if to a water-place. Rather, one should stand up and adjust the lower robe. For one going by boat, the proper conduct is: if there is a latrine, it should be done there. A piece of wood should be placed in between, so that [the excrement] falls there first. If that is not possible, at the very least, one's own finger should be placed [to direct it]. If there is no latrine, [it] should be thrown out with a basin or a vessel. If [waste is] seen near a <s>stūpa</s> or a <s>Saṃgha</s> building, it should be removed. Now, if two are walking — an elder and a junior — the junior should clean it up. But if he is lazy, negligent, stubborn, or unwilling to learn, then [the elder] himself should clean it up. This monk has been ill for a long time. The physician prescribes: 'At mealtime, he should be given a strong purgative.' What should be done? If it is his own excrement, that itself serves as the medicine [ingredient] for him. But if it is another's excrement, it should be obtained [from them]. Having washed it with water, having strained it through a dense cloth, [offering it to] that monk with jasmine flowers — if it cannot be given [directly], one should say: 'Venerable one, the smell of this medicine is like that of excrement. Let it not be disagreeable to you — drink it if you wish to live.' Thus should all conduct themselves regarding all excrement. One who does not so conduct himself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

— having given the <s>nidāna</s> (narrative occasion) in full — now a certain <s>bhikṣu</s>, pressed by flatulence, hitching up his lower robe, entered the latrine. And there another <s>bhikṣu</s> had entered earlier. He then said: 'Do not, venerable one, defecate on me!' The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus at the latrine. And how should one conduct oneself at the latrine? It is not proper for a <s>bhikṣu</s> to wait until he is pressed by flatulence. Rather, one should go to the latrine as a matter of routine. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s> is suddenly pressed by flatulence, it is not proper to enter the latrine silently while hitching up the lower robe. Rather, one should enter snapping the fingers. If someone has entered earlier there, he should snap his fingers in reply. By this one should wait until he has risen. But if one is [urgently] pressed, one should announce by snapping the fingers. And one should turn away. And space should be given to him. And he should sit down facing away. Space should be given.

children.translated_text: (I.p.91) II.9 Ms. 17b4 (J. 78.7); Ch.504c18 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>, the Teacher of gods and humans. Having given the background in detail: Now those monks were passing wind indiscriminately. The people grumbled: 'Look, sirs, these wretched ascetics! Just like camels, oxen, donkeys, or goats — these wretched ascetics pass wind indiscriminately. They are lost and fallen — from where is their asceticism?' This matter was heard by the monks; the monks reported it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, monks, that people grumble [thus]? Therefore, a breathing-room (<s>praśvāsakuṭī</s>) should be built.' Now, the monk having it built — it is not proper to have it built to the north or to the east of the monastery. Rather, it should be built to the south or to the west, avoiding the wind-path, and it should be built above the water drainage. On stone or brick, a plastered pit should be dug. A hole should be made in the middle. It should be placed above the water drainage. With good plaster, it should be coated all around. A wall should be made all around, so that the foul air goes out to the outside. Having washed, [the room] should be anointed with oil. [It should be used] by the newest [monk], or by the designated one, or in sequential order, or by whomever [needs it]. // * // This is the origin of the matter. //

children.translated_text: both should relieve themselves. Furthermore, it is not proper to sit [in the privy] with the head covered, or with the hands lowered, or while chewing a tooth-stick. Rather, with the upper robe over one shoulder, having placed the tooth-stick to one side, one should sit down. Nor is it proper to sit there while meditating (<s>dhyāna</s>), or reciting, or absorbed in the meditation on impurity (<s>aśubhasamāpatti</s>). Rather, having relieved oneself, one should immediately get up. Now this monk, seated in meditation, having finished at the privy, should get up and go to the privy [in advance next time]. But if he is pressed by the need to urinate, it is not proper to go [relieving oneself] while urinating on his thighs like a camel, or a bull, or a donkey. Rather, having sat down to one side, he should relieve himself. Now if he is seen by another monk, it is not proper to say: 'Who is this? What is this? Let him not be ashamed.' And having relieved himself, if that spot of ground is hard-packed earth, it should be scraped clean with a stick or a potsherd. But if the ground is cultivated soil, it should be washed. Then an oil-application or a scent-application should be given. But if there are no means, at the very least a cow-dung application should be given. But if there is no privy, in one corner [of the premises], a urinal-pot for the whole <s>saṃgha</s> should be placed, with a perforated bowl placed on top of it.

The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>, the Teacher of gods and humans. Having given the background in detail: Now another monk, seated in meditation (<s>prahāṇa</s>), being pressed by the need to urinate, went to the privy. Lifting up his lower robe, he was about to relieve himself. But there a monk who had entered earlier was already relieving himself. He said: 'Please do not urinate on me, venerable one!' The monks heard of this matter and reported it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus regarding the privy. It is not proper for a monk to wait until he is [desperately] pressed by the need to urinate. Rather, as a matter of [regular] habit, one should go to the privy. Nor is it proper to enter the privy without making a sound. Rather,

A perforated bowl should be placed on top of the pot; on top of the perforated bowl, a plug or gourd-stopper should be placed. When climbing up [to bed], the bowl or pot should be placed carefully beneath the bed and firmly settled so that [it] does not [tip over]. children.translated_text: one should go. Placing the pot in front, one should relieve oneself. Whoever is one's second companion, he should stand behind with his back turned. This <s>bhikṣu</s> travels the same road with the caravan and has relieved himself. It is not proper to relieve oneself on the road, lest people complain: "Who has relieved himself on the road? It looks like blood." Rather, one should relieve oneself in a secluded spot, going aside from the road to a private place. And it is not proper to do so downwind, lest the caravan be troubled by the smell. It should be done against the wind. Now when the caravan has halted and there is need, one should go to a secluded spot after rising. One should not rise without giving notice, lest one be struck [and killed] as a thief or robber. Rather, one should rise after giving notice. And it should not be done downwind; it should be done against the wind. When going by boat, if there is a need, if there is a latrine, it should be done there. But if there is no latrine, it should be done in a vessel and discarded.

Lest outsiders relieve themselves on the outside of the pot. There a plug or a gourd-stopper should be placed. Having relieved oneself there, [the waste] should be deposited in the pot. It is not proper to throw feces or phlegm and nasal discharge into it. It should be emptied. The novice — or whoever is on [cleaning] duty — if there is [waste] left over from the body, it is not proper to discard [it] in a frequented place, lest the whole <s>saṃgha</s> be troubled by the smell. children.translated_text: Now if a <s>bhikṣu</s> is ill with jaundice and the doctor says: "Give him fresh urine to drink" — what should be done? If it is one's own urine, discarding the first and last portions, the middle portion should be taken. Such is the receipt of it. But if it is from another person, discarding the first and last portions, it should be taken and afterward offered [to the patient]. If jasmine blossoms cannot be given to that sick person [to mask the taste], one should say: "Drink this medicine prescribed by the <s>Buddha</s>, if you wish to live." Thus one should conduct oneself regarding excretions. One who does not so conduct himself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). ////

children.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the <s>nidāna</s> (narrative occasion) in full: now a certain <s>bhikṣu</s> was chewing a tooth-stick. While chewing, he used up the tooth-stick completely. Then, having seen the <s>Bhagavān</s>, out of respect for the <s>Bhagavān</s> he swallowed it all. Then he became sick. The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'So you chew the tooth-stick completely, leaving nothing? Therefore, four finger-breadths of the tooth-stick should be left as remainder.' Now if <s>bhikṣus</s> dwell in a forest lodging and a suitable attendant is hard to find, what should be done? Large tooth-sticks should be prepared. Then, after the <s>bhikṣu</s> has chewed the tooth-stick, the brush-end should be cut off with a knife. Having washed it, it should be kept. The next day, one should chew again in the same manner. One should chew in this way until four finger-breadths of the tooth-stick remain, then it should be discarded. That <s>bhikṣu</s> who chews the tooth-stick completely commits a <s>Vinaya</s> transgression. While chewing a tooth-stick, it is not proper to chew at a <s>stūpa</s> shrine or in the assembly of the <s>Saṃgha</s>. But if the <s>bhikṣu</s> is sick — having been bled, or having taken a purgative, or having drunk ghee — even if he chews a tooth-stick in the <s>Saṃgha</s> assembly, there is no offence. While chewing a tooth-stick, it is not proper to spit phlegm in all directions, or to shake the brush-end and spray in all directions. Rather, phlegm should be spat into a basin, a bowl, a corner, or a folded container. The brush-end should be held with the left hand. Afterward it should be discarded to one side. While chewing a tooth-stick, it is not proper to chew in the service hall, the fire-hall, the dining hall, the preparation hall, the preparation hut, in the midst of the <s>Saṃgha</s>, in front of one's preceptor or teacher, or in front of senior <s>bhikṣus</s>. It is not proper to chew a tooth-stick in front of women. It is not proper to chew with the head covered, or with hands hanging down, at a <s>cetiya</s> (shrine), or in a shrine-pavilion or multi-storied building. With one shoulder bared, one should chew to one side. It is not proper, having chewed a tooth-stick, to lick the tongue through the middle [of the stick] like a sensualist. But if the <s>bhikṣu</s> wishes to clean his tongue, it should be scraped with the brush-end. It is not proper to chew a tooth-stick for the purpose of beautification. Rather, a tooth-stick should be chewed for the purpose of removing bad odor. But if no tooth-stick is available, the teeth should be rubbed with charcoal or with unripe <s>āmalaka</s> fruit. At the very least, a finger should serve as a tooth-stick. That <s>bhikṣu</s> who does not chew a tooth-stick at all commits a <s>Vinaya</s> transgression. When this <s>bhikṣu</s> pays homage to a <s>cetiya</s> and sees a spittoon, it should be cleaned. If there are two persons, the junior one should carry it away. But if the junior one is lax and indolent, the senior one should carry it away. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the tooth-stick. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

  Thus should one conduct oneself regarding lodgings.

III.1 Ms.20a6 (J.91.1); Ch.505c1 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the <s>nidāna</s> (narrative occasion) in full: seeing five reasons, the <s>Tathāgatas</s>, <s>Arhats</s>, Perfectly Awakened Ones undertake a five-day tour of the monastery dwellings. What five? [To see] whether my disciples are not devoted to work, not delighting in work, not engaged in the pursuit of devotion to work — in detail, up to: the <s>Bhagavān</s> saw, on his five-day tour of the monastery dwellings, walking about and inspecting, a certain <s>bhikṣu</s> sewing a robe spread out on the ground. The <s>Bhagavān</s>, knowing, asked: 'What is this, <s>bhikṣu</s>?' He said: '<s>Bhagavān</s>, I am sewing this robe.'
  The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'So you sew a robe spread out on the ground? Therefore, a <s>kaṭhina</s> (sewing frame) should be made. When a <s>bhikṣu</s> has a <s>kaṭhina</s> made, it should be twelve cubits in length and eight cubits in width. It should be woven of bamboo, reeds, plough-shafts, stalks, pots, <s>rohiṣa</s> grass, or twine or cord. When a <s>bhikṣu</s> wishes to sew a robe, he should set up the <s>kaṭhina</s> in the service hall, the fire-hall, the multi-storied building, or the meditation hall, and sew the robe. Having spread the <s>kaṭhina</s>, having washed his feet, having sat cross-legged on the <s>kaṭhina</s>, he should sew the robe. If another also wishes to sew, he too, having washed his feet, should sit cross-legged on the <s>kaṭhina</s> and sew the robe. If while seated he extends his feet outward and passes urine [accidentally], there is no offence. If the <s>bhikṣu</s> wishes to wash his feet, it is not proper to step on the <s>kaṭhina</s> with unwashed feet. Rather, placing his feet on the outside of the <s>kaṭhina</s>, he should sew the robe. When the robe has been sewn, the <s>kaṭhina</s> should be rolled up, two pegs should be driven into the wall, [the <s>kaṭhina</s>] should be tied with a rope and hung up there. If another also wishes to sew, he too should spread the <s>kaṭhina</s> and sew the robe in the same manner. It is not proper to clean dye or cow-dung or robes on the <s>kaṭhina</s>. Rather, robes alone should be sewn [on it]. It is not proper to neglect the <s>kaṭhina</s>, [leaving it] suspended or broken, being destroyed by wind and sun, or being rained upon, or being defecated on by birds. Rather, from time to time it should be tied up, from time to time repaired. If no <s>kaṭhina</s> is available, the robe should be placed on top of a bed or a seat and sewn. If even that is not possible, in the meditation hall, or the service hall, or the circular pavilion, a spot should be plastered with cow-dung and the robe sewn. At the very least, the robe should be placed on top of one's knees and sewn. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the <s>kaṭhina</s>. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

children.translated_text: If it has a clay roof, a clay lump should be provided. If brick-roofed, bricks should be provided. If tile-roofed, tiles should be provided. If potsherd-roofed, potsherds should be provided. If plank-roofed, planks should be provided. If plaster-roofed, a plaster lump should be provided. From time to time it should be cleaned. Creepers should be removed. Rat burrows should be tamped down. Uneven ground should be leveled. Puddles should be filled. Drains should be provided. If the plaster is peeling, the old [plaster] should be stripped off, and it should be re-plastered, re-coated, and polished smooth. If the floor is tiled, it should be re-covered with dust or gravel. If the dwelling is dusty, from time to time it should be sprinkled, swept, and cow-dung plaster should be applied. Creepers should be removed. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the dwelling. If one does not so conduct oneself, one transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

III.3 Ms.21a4 (J.95.4); Ch.505c17 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail, seeing five purposes — given in full — the <s>Bhagavān</s>, while walking on a five-day tour of inspection, [saw] the dwellings sagging, falling apart, with plaster peeling off, unclean, unrepaired.
The <s>Bhagavān</s>, though knowing, asked: 'Why are these dwellings, monks, sagging, falling apart, with plaster peeling off, unclean, unrepaired? Therefore, thus should one conduct oneself regarding the dwellings. There are three [types of] dwellings: superior, middle, and inferior. A superior dwelling has [plastered] flooring, a dark-colored ceiling, whitewashed walls, and is well-crafted. Thus is the superior [dwelling]. What then is the middle? A middle dwelling has dark-colored walls and is well-crafted, but does not have a [white] ceiling or whitewashed [walls]. Thus is the middle [dwelling]. What then is the inferior? [It merely] has flooring, dark-colored [walls] — it does not have a [white] ceiling, whitewashed [walls], or well-crafted walls. Thus is the inferior [dwelling]. In the superior dwelling, it is not proper to drag in beds or stools there. Rather, four supports should be made, lest the floor be damaged. Having brought [the furniture] in, [it] should be placed upon the supports there. If there are no supports, the feet should be bound with cloth wrappings. If a stool is brought in, for the stool likewise, [and for] a chair or tripod — their feet should be bound with cloth wrappings. Nor is it proper there to light a small lamp or to bring in a lamp. But if a monk wishes to prepare his bed, even if he brings in a lamp — no offence. Having prepared the bed, it [the flame] should be extinguished and removed. Nor is it proper there to wash the feet, wash the hands, or wash the face. Nor is it proper to walk about on the walking-path there. But if a monk is ill, even if he goes back and forth five or six times — no offence. Nor is it proper [to walk] in one direction only; rather, one should walk all around. And whatever [debris from] sweeping

When this monk has gone for the day-rest and is walking on the walkway — if the monk has a phlegmatic condition — if he walks along spitting here and there, he incurs a transgression of the <s>Vinaya</s>. Rather, having spat, one should rub it in with the foot. At the head of the walkway, a turned-over vessel, or sand in a raised bowl, should be placed; one should spit into that. When one goes [on the alms-round], one should spit to one side. When seated in meditation and bothered by phlegm, one should make [a ball] in the fold of a sandal and rub it into the ground.

III.4 Ms.21b7 (J.97.3); Ch.505c29 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the five reasons in full, up to: the <s>Bhagavān</s> saw, while walking around and inspecting on the five-day monastery tour, that the walls of the dwellings had been ruined by dried spittle and dried nasal mucus, with strands of nasal mucus hanging [from them]. The <s>Bhagavān</s>, though knowing, asked: 'Why, monks, are the walls of the dwellings [stained] with dried spittle and dried nasal mucus, with strands hanging [from them]?' Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus regarding spitting. And how should one conduct oneself regarding spitting?

children.translated_text: III.6 Ms.23a4 (J.104.4); Ch.506b13 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>ṣaḍvārgikas</s> (Group of Six monks) criticized gruel in various ways. Some [gruel] they disparaged, some they praised. When it was thin, they said: "Ha ha ha! This is no gruel — this is the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, this is the <s>Sarayū</s>, the <s>Ajiravatī</s>, the <s>Mahī</s>, the <s>Mahāmahī</s>!" — [pointing] with knuckle-fists — "One must search for rice grains in this!" But when it was thick, they said: "Ha ha ha! This is no gruel — this is curds, this is thick drink, this is a chopping-block to be cut with a saw!" Those <s>bhikṣus</s> were upset, tongue-tied, perplexed, and speechless. The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Summon the <s>ṣaḍvārgikas</s>." They were summoned and questioned about the same. They said: "Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>." The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus regarding gruel. And how should one conduct oneself regarding gruel? When the time for gruel has been announced, one should know: is this gruel for both <s>Saṃgha</s> assemblies, for a particular assembly, for a cell-group, or for those invited? If it is for both assemblies, all should go. If for a particular assembly, that assembly should go. If for a cell-group, those cell-members should go. If for those invited, those invited should go. As a matter of course, a <s>bhikṣu</s> should first chew a tooth-stick, wash his face, clean his hands, take his bowl, and sit down. It is not proper to receive gruel while wearing sandals, or with head covered, or fully wrapped. Rather, having removed sandals, with one shoulder bared, the gruel should be received. But if a disciplinary action has been assigned, the ankle-strap should be loosened, permission for the second-time allowance should be requested, and then one should go. When [the gruel] is served to those seated in proper order, one should accept as is proper. If the gruel is thin, one should not say: "Ha ha ha! This is the <s>Gaṅgā</s>" — and so on up to the <s>Mahī</s> and <s>Candrabhāgā</s>. But if it is too thick, one should not say: "This is not gruel — this is rice, this should be broken with a stick-seat." Rather, whatever is given, such should be accepted — it is the donor's prerogative, not the recipient's. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s> is weak from old age or weak from illness, or if it is extremely cold or extremely hot, and the <s>bhikṣu</s> cannot chew a tooth-stick, nor wash his face, nor clean his hands, the bowl should be given to the one next [in line], saying: "Venerable one, take this, my share of gruel." When it has been received, then it should be consumed. Those who delay and criticize or praise the gruel incur a <s>Vinaya</s> transgression. Thus one should conduct oneself regarding gruel. One who does not so conduct himself —

children.text: abhisamācārikān dharmmān atikramati // * //
children.translated_text: transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). ////

III.7 Ms.23b3 (J.106.8); Ch.506b28 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: Now another <s>bhikṣu</s>, a <s>yogācāra</s> (meditation practitioner), was seated on <s>Vaideha</s> mountain, [thinking:] "I shall concentrate my mind." Another <s>bhikṣu</s> came and stood in front of him. Due to that hindrance (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>), his mind did not go into concentration. That <s>yogācāra</s> reported the matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Summon that <s>bhikṣu</s>." He was summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Is it true, <s>bhikṣu</s>, that another <s>yogācāra</s> was seated on <s>Vaideha</s> mountain, [trying to] concentrate his mind, and you came and stood in front of him, and due to that hindrance his mind did not go into concentration?" He said: "Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>." The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Wrongly done by you, <s>bhikṣu</s>, that you stand in front of a <s>yogācāra</s> <s>bhikṣu</s>. Therefore, one should stand thus. And how should one stand? It is not proper for a <s>bhikṣu</s> to stand in front of a <s>yogācāra</s> <s>bhikṣu</s>. Nor is it proper to stand near a boundary-wall or beside a prison, execution-hall, or slaughter-house. It is not proper to stand in a place that is too secluded or too exposed. Rather, in a place that is sheltered yet visible,

III.9 Ms.24a6 (J.109.4); Ch.507a4 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s> (Group of Six monks) sat in the meditation hall in camel-posture, striking their neighbors with their knees. The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon the <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, <s>bhikṣus</s>, <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>, that you sit in camel-posture in the meditation hall, striking your neighbors with your knees?' They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'You have done wrong, <s>bhikṣus</s>, <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>. So you sit in camel-posture in the meditation hall. Therefore, it is not proper to sit in camel-posture in the meditation hall.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed those <s>bhikṣus</s>: 'Sit thus, <s>bhikṣus</s>, as the <s>nāgas</s> (serpent kings) of the <s>Himavat</s> (Himalayas): one <s>nāga</s> sits surrounded by two <s>nāgas</s>; two <s>nāgas</s> sit surrounded by four <s>nāgas</s>; four by eight, eight by sixteen, sixteen by thirty-two,

children.translated_text: placing foot upon foot, placing the tip of the tongue at the palate, extending the fingers along the body, placing the right arm at the head, extending the left arm along the body — upon awakening too, one lifts the front of the body and looks at the back of the body. If one sees that the limbs have changed position, one is displeased; and if one sees that the limbs have changed position, one is pleased in mind, delighted. Even a monk, when preparing the bed, should prepare it on the right [side] — it should be done such that one lies in the proper position on the right side. It is not proper to prepare the bed on the left [side]; the right-side bed should be prepared. Below the robe-rack, during the first watch of the night, one should pass the time engaged in study, recitation, standing, and walking meditation. During the middle watch of the night, the lion's posture (<s>siṃhaśeyyā</s>) should be adopted on the right side — placing foot upon foot, placing the tip of the tongue at the palate, placing the right arm at the head, extending the left arm along the body, bearing in mind the perception of rising — one should not turn over; from that time until sunrise one should sleep. During the last watch of the night, one should pass the time cross-legged, engaged in study, or standing and walking [meditation]. Now if a monk is a restless sleeper, turning from side to side — no offence. [If he is] weakened by old age or weakened by illness, [or if] there is a boil or an abscess on the right side — even if he lies on the left side — no offence. It is not proper to prepare the bed with feet toward a <s>stūpa</s> (reliquary), or with feet toward the <s>saṃgha</s>, or with feet toward seniors, or with feet toward the preceptor (<s>upādhyāya</s>) and teacher (<s>ācārya</s>). Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the bed. If one does not so conduct oneself, one transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). * ////

III.10 Ms.24b6 (J.111.7); Ch.507a15 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. — the venerable group-of-six — the visitors were seen. They asked: 'Venerable ones, how did you enter?' They said: 'We entered by climbing over.' They then said: 'So you entered the dwelling by climbing over!' The visitors too then said: 'And you were sitting behind the dwelling with the door fastened, breaking the ridge-beam!' They then quarreled. They went to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'This is not proper. It is not proper for resident monks to fasten the dwelling's door and sit behind the dwelling breaking the ridge-beam. Nor is it proper for visiting monks to enter the dwelling by climbing over. Therefore, thus should visiting monks conduct themselves, and thus should resident monks conduct themselves. How then should visiting monks conduct themselves? When monks arrive as visitors, all sandals, footwear, and coverings should be set aside.

children.translated_text: Lest, through not seeing [it], one [later] lament: 'My bowl and robes have been stolen! Stolen!' — this is what should be done by one who is traveling. If there is a ford, the junior monks should go in front, testing the ford. But if there is danger from wild beasts or danger from robbers, the old and the young should be placed in the middle and one should travel [thus]. But if the robbers are inclined to be respectful, the elders should go in front, so that [the robbers], seeing them, might let [the group] pass undisturbed out of respect. If one must travel through the middle of a village or city, it is not proper to go around the city shrines doing circumambulation to the right, or to the left. Rather, one should go by the straight road. When they arrive at their lodging for the night, two or three junior monks should be sent ahead: 'Go ahead and prepare comfortable accommodation for the <s>saṃgha</s> — foot-oil, sugar-water drink, lodging, and morning meal.' By those [monks], having wrapped [their robes], having tied the knot-fastener, having announced themselves, [the village] should be entered. Having entered, having requested, comfortable provisions for the <s>saṃgha</s> should be procured — foot-oil, afternoon allowable [food], and morning meal should be begged for and secured. Having obtained lodging, if there is a stream, or a river, or a pond, or a lotus-tank, or a well, there the feet should be washed, the upper robe should be draped, and having called to one another, one should enter [the lodging]. But if there is sugar-water drink, the afternoon allowable [food] should be consumed right there before entering, lest [the laity] see and say: 'These renunciants are indulging themselves.' But if [one's load] is divided, having shared [it], one should enter. If it is an open dwelling, one may enter without announcing — there is no offence. If one cannot go by any other [route] and there is an opening from a lane — there is no offence. If there is a village-adjacent dwelling, one should go there. But if there is a forest-dwelling, one should go there. When entering the monastery, the feet should be washed in the lotus-tank, or the pond, or the stream before entering. If [one's load] is divided, having shared [it], one should enter. When doing circumambulation of the shrines, the sandals should be removed, held by a wooden [stick], and one should enter. Nor should one enter with loud noise and great clamor. Nor should the resident monks be taunted: 'Ha, ha! Even now you are living here! You old logs, you, <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>! You are serpent-kings! Here you were born, here you will die! Those jackals are born who will eat your flesh!' Nor should the resident monks taunt [the visitors]: 'Ha, ha! Free and gone five years and you show up just as you left!' Nor should one say: 'Who is this? How many rains? Get up!' Nor should one say: 'Who has meals? Are there no guests? Whose meal or refreshment or morning meal is it tomorrow?' Nor should the resident monks sit with the door shut, sharing out crow-portions [among themselves]. Now when they are doing clay-work in the afternoon, whatever helpers there are — monastery attendants, or novices, or whoever is on duty — he should be told: 'Guard the door and stay.' But if the dwelling is unlocked, one should enter. But if it is latched, the door should be opened with the door-lever and one should enter. Having done circumambulation of the monastery, one should come to where the seating arrangement for the monks is. There, a new [monk], having set down his robe-bundle, his water-pot, and his sandals, should ask the resident monks: 'Venerable one, where is the foot-washing [place]? Where is the proper water-vessel? Where is the improper water-vessel?' If they point [them out], having washed the feet at the foot-washing [place], having cleaned the hands from the improper vessel, having rinsed from the proper vessel, then the shrine should be worshipped. Having worshipped the shrine, one should go where the resident monks are. Having approached, it is not proper to say: 'I pay respects!' Rather, one should say: 'Venerable one, I wish to pay respects.' The resident monks

children.translated_text: is more senior, the resident monk should rise and pay homage at the feet, and a seat should be given. But if the resident monk is more senior, having inquired about health and done [the same], a seat should be given. When [the visitor] is rested, he should be asked: 'Venerable one, is there a dwelling available for [one of] such-and-such rains?' If he says it is available, a dwelling should be given, with a bed, stool, mat, square cushion, pillow, and bolster. Nor is it proper for visiting monks to insult and ridicule the resident monks: 'Venerable one, even now you are living here! You so-and-so! You know who the jackals are who will eat your flesh!' Rather, they should be encouraged [and told]: 'Venerable one, a fine thing is being done! The monastery is being kept up! Activity is generated! The families [of donors] are being cultivated!' At the proper time, having washed and anointed the feet, having lit the lamp, having prepared the bed, one should retire. Nor is it proper, at dawn the very next day, to go straight into the refectory upon waking: 'Venerable one, what is ready? What is being cooked? What are the meal-arrangements?' Rather, having risen early, having put on the lower robe, having draped the upper robe, having washed the hands, one should take the bowl and enter. But if there is a benefit at that dwelling, or there are dwelling-meals, the resident monks should say: 'Venerable ones, do not go for alms; you will eat right here.' But if there are alms-food portions for the visiting monks, alms-food should be assigned. But if there are meal-portions, meal-portions should be assigned. But if there are no meal-portions, the resident monks should say: 'Venerable ones, wait; we will go together for alms.' Then they should enter together. Now then,

children.translated_text: for resident monks to say: "Oh ho! These boats! Five-year sufferers! Born of ascetic mothers!" Rather, visitors should be welcomed with hospitality: "Come, venerable ones! Welcome, venerable ones! How glad we are [to see you], venerable ones! Are you not tired, not weary? Wash your feet, clean your hands, drink water, rest." If they have arrived before the meal, they should be offered before-meal food. If they have arrived at mealtime, they should be offered the meal. If they have arrived at the wrong time, they should be offered what is allowable at the wrong time. A cell should be assigned — a bed, stool, mat, square cushion, brush, and pillow should be designated. They should be offered foot-ointment. From the next day on, if there is an external meal or a favor [available], one should say: "Venerable ones, do not go on alms-round; you will eat right here." But if there are no meals, alms-food portions should be assigned to the visitors. But if [the monastery] relies on alms-rounds — when the visitors have returned from their alms-round to the monastery, if the resident monks have side-dishes, snacks, or oil, they should share with the visitors. But if even that is not available, at the very least, whatever better alms-food there is should be offered to the visitors as a courtesy. The resident monks should inform [them] of everything, saying: "Venerable ones, do not enter such-and-such a family. The bowl-turning-over [penalty] has been agreed upon.

children.translated_text: at a later time, the two met. The elder asked: "Venerable one, how long [have you been here]?" When told the time of arrival — "this long, that long" — he said: "Venerable one, you have been here this long since your arrival, yet you have not come to pay respects at my feet." He then said: "I did pay respects at your feet, but you did not greet me in return." He said: "When? What?" He said: "On such-and-such a day, when you were having a dispute with such-and-such a <s>bhikṣu</s>, at that time I paid respects at your feet." He then said: "Venerable one, you pay respects at my feet while I am having a dispute?" He said: "Even so, when I pay respects at your feet, you do not greet me in return." They disputed and went to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "It is not proper for a visiting monk to pay respects at the feet of a resident monk who is having a dispute. Nor is it proper not to greet one who is paying respects at one's feet. Therefore, thus should feet be respected, and thus should one greet in return. And how should feet be respected and how should one greet in return? Now this visiting <s>bhikṣu</s> has arrived. He has an acquaintance among the <s>bhikṣus</s>. But that [acquaintance] is having a dispute with another <s>bhikṣu</s>. It is not proper to pay respects at his feet at that time. [Nor is it proper] when he is seated at the privy — it is not proper to pay respects at his feet at that time. Likewise when he is urinating, chewing a tooth-stick, bathing, wearing only one garment, doing meal-duty, doing the before-meal duty, climbing to the second floor, going in haste — it is not proper to pay respects at his feet at that time. Nor is it proper [to do so] when he is doing clay-work.

children.translated_text: abbreviated // [It is not proper to bow] while one is firing a bowl, while washing robes, while reciting the dyeing [formula], while sewing robes, while dyeing, or while doing cloth-work, while washing feet, while washing hands, while worshipping a shrine, while cleaning the bowl, or while inhaling medicinal fumes, or while applying collyrium to the eyes, while reading a book, while writing a book, while going to the latrine, or [while one is] naked, or [wearing only] a single garment. Rather, at the time when [the elder] is comfortably seated, at that moment one should approach and venerate his feet with the head. One should bow in the crab-clasp manner. [It is not proper to bow] in darkness, or while one is giving instruction, or while one is reciting, or while one is dressing, or while one is putting on the upper robe, or while one is going in haste — it is not proper. With the body covered, it is not proper. With the hands hanging down, it is not proper. While wearing sandals and making salutation, it is not proper — to bow with the knees or with the shins. Rather, the feet should be venerated. When venerating the feet, one should check: if someone has a wound, or a boil or a blister, one should not press [the feet] suddenly. Rather, one should bow in such a way that it does not cause pain when venerating the feet. One should not sit like a ram when venerating the feet. Rather, one should exchange greetings: 'Welcome, venerable ones! We rejoice at your coming! Are you not tired? Are you not weary? Wash your feet, clean your hands, take rest.' If he has arrived before the meal, he should be offered the before-meal [provisions]. If he arrives at the [proper] time, he should be offered the meal. If he arrives at the improper time, he should be offered the after-hours [provisions]. If he wishes to stay, the bowl and robes should be put away, and a dwelling should be assigned. But if he wishes to go, he says: 'I will go elsewhere.' One should say: 'Go then.' Thus should the feet be venerated. Thus should one exchange greetings. One who does not practice thus transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

children.translated_text: IV.5 Ms.27b6 (J.126.1); Ch.510b28 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: Now the venerable <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s> (Group of Six monks) addressed [others] using lay speech: 'Mother! Grandmother! Sir! Master! Father! Hey! Ho ho! What do you say?' The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon the <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, monks, <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>, that you address [others] using lay speech — "Mother! Grandmother! Sir! Master! Father! Hey! Ho ho! What do you say?"' They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'So you address [others] using lay speech. Therefore, it is not proper to address [others] using lay speech. Rather, one should exchange greetings [properly].' Now the venerable <s>Upāli</s>, knowing the right time, the right occasion, and the right moment, approached the <s>Bhagavān</s> and asked: 'How, <s>Bhagavān</s>, should elder monks be addressed by junior monks?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: '[They should say:] "Venerable sir" (<s>ālapaye</s>), or "Reverend sir" (<s>bhante</s>), or "Long-lived one" (<s>āyuṣman</s>).' Then the elder asked the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'How, <s>Bhagavān</s>, should junior monks be addressed by elder monks?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'By [their] name, or by [their] clan (<s>gotra</s>), or by [their] seniority.' Now this monk's <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor) or <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) calls [him]. It is not proper to respond with lay speech: 'Hey! Ho ho!' Rather, [the preceptor/teacher] should be addressed by name or by clan. By him too, it is not proper to speak using lay language: 'Ha! What do you say?' Rather, one should say: 'I salute the <s>upādhyāya</s>' or 'the <s>ācārya</s>. What do you command? What shall I do?' When an elder monk calls, it is not proper to respond with 'Ha!' Rather, one should say: 'Noble sir' or 'Reverend sir' or 'Long-lived one — what do you command? What shall I do?' This monk wishes to address his mother, father, or sister. It is not proper to address [them as]: 'Mother!' or 'Grandmother!' or 'Madam!' Rather, they should be addressed as 'Relative' (<s>sālohita</s>). Now if the monk's father or sister addresses him, it is not proper to respond: 'Ha! What do you say?' Rather, one should say: 'Relative, what do you command? What shall I do?' This monk wishes to address <s>upāsikās</s> (lay devotees), <s>dānapatīs</s> (donors), or the <s>vihārasvāminī</s> (mistress of the monastery). It is not proper [to address them as]: 'Mother!' or 'Grandmother!' or 'Madam!' Rather, they should be addressed as '<s>upāsikā</s>' (lay devotee), or '<s>dānapati</s>' (donor), or '<s>vihārasvāminī</s>' (mistress of the monastery). The monk wishes to address an <s>upāsaka</s> (male lay devotee) or a <s>dānapati</s> (donor). It is not proper [to say]: 'Sir!' or 'Master!' or 'Long-lived one!' Rather, [one should say] '<s>dānapati</s>' (donor). If a monk is addressed by them, it is not proper to respond: 'Ha! What do you say?' Rather, one should say: 'Relative, what do you command? What shall I do?' Those who address [others] or speak using this lay language incur a transgression of the <s>Vinaya</s> (monastic discipline). If a woman or a man is elderly, one should not address them as one would one's parents. Rather, one should say 'Elder, Elder.' But if someone asks: 'Who is your <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor)? Who is your <s>ācārya</s> (teacher)?' one should not say simply: 'So-and-so is my teacher, so-and-so is my preceptor.' Rather, one should say: 'For the sake of the matter, I take the name: so-and-so is my <s>upādhyāya</s>, so-and-so is my <s>ācārya</s>.' Thus should one address [others]. Thus should one speak. One who does not practice thus transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

IV.6 Ms.28a7 (J.128.14); Ch.510c19 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: Now the <s>Kṣatriya</s> (warrior-noble) assembly had gathered, [saying:] 'We shall conduct our business.' The venerable <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s> came and sat in their midst. With them seated [there], they could not conduct their business. They grumbled: 'Look, sirs, we ourselves have gathered to conduct our business, yet these wretched ascetics too have come and sat in our midst. They are lost and fallen — from where is their asceticism?' The monks heard [this]. The monks reported [it] to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, monks, <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>, that the <s>Kṣatriya</s> assembly had gathered [saying:] "We shall conduct our business," and you went and sat in their midst, and with you seated [there] they could not conduct their business, and they grumbled: "Look, sirs, we ourselves are seated to conduct our business, yet these wretched ascetics too have come and sat in our midst — they are lost and fallen — from where is their asceticism?"' They then grumbled: 'Look, sirs, we had gathered to conduct our business. These petty ascetics came and sat down in the middle! Ruined! Fallen! What asceticism do they have?' The <s>bhikṣus</s> heard this matter. The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported [it] to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, <s>bhikṣus</s>, <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>, that the householder assembly had gathered, [saying:] "We will conduct our business"?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> related the entire matter in detail, up to: 'Look, sirs, we had gathered to conduct our business. These petty ascetics came and sat down in the middle! Ruined! Fallen! What asceticism do they have?' They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'
  The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should a householder assembly be approached. And how should a householder assembly be approached? If this <s>bhikṣu</s> has some business in the householder assembly, it is not proper to enter hastily. Rather, those who are the chief householders there, they should first be visited. One should say: "Long-lived ones, is there any business in the householder assembly? May I enter or may I not?" If they say: "Venerable sir, do not enter," it is not proper to enter. But if they say: "Enter," one should enter. It is not proper to approach the householder assembly while carrying an umbrella or wearing bound sandals. Rather, having set aside the umbrella and sandals to one side, one should approach the householder assembly. One should not set [them] down within the line of sight. Rather,

They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should the heretic assembly (<s>tīrthika-parṣā</s>) be approached. When a monk has some business with an assembly of heretics, it is not proper for a monk to approach the heretic assembly by simply going and coming. Rather, as a matter of course, the senior monks should first be consulted. One should say: "Venerable one, I have some business with the heretic assembly — shall I go or shall I not?" If they say: "Do not go" — it is not proper to go. But if they say: "Go" — then one should approach. And it is not proper to act hastily in the matter of seating. Rather, whatever seat is available, one should sit on that. Nor is it proper to disparage or reproach [them, saying:] "The heretics are faithless! The heretics are shameless! The heretics have no moral dread! The heretics hold wrong views! The heretics are lazy and of inferior effort! The heretics are of poor wisdom!" Rather, one should speak thus: "Among all renunciants, there should be no reproach; some may have attained the three knowledges; some are learned." Whoever is praiseworthy, him one should praise; one should speak of their virtues, not faults. One should say: "Difficult is the abandonment of the householder's life. Difficult is self-restraint. Difficult is dwelling in the forest."

The <s>saṃgha</s> should settle that business according to <s>Dharma</s>, <s>Vinaya</s>, and the Teacher's instruction. Having settled [it], that monk should be asked: 'Venerable one, is this matter settled?' If he says: 'It is settled,' he should be told: 'Venerable one, this matter has been settled by the complete <s>saṃgha</s> in agreement. Do not reopen [it] for further action, and do not go again to the assembly [about it]. The <s>saṃgha</s> will examine you further [if you do].' Having done as is comfortable, one should go. IV.10 Ms.30a5 (J.136.12); Ch.511b3 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now when a monk has business with the noble assembly (<s>ārya-parṣā</s>), it is not proper for a monk to speak his matter by simply going and coming. Rather, as a matter of course, the preceptor (<s>upādhyāya</s>) or teacher (<s>ācārya</s>) should first be addressed.

The village-dwellers said: "And you come too late." Then, from the next day, the forest-dwellers got up early in the morning and took up all the food portions. Then the village-dwellers, at the proper time, went to the lay families and said: "Lay sister, give [us food]." [They said:] "The food has been taken up." "By whom?" "By the forest-dwellers." They then said to those forest-dwellers: "Venerable ones, why have you taken up all the food?" They said: "Because you just strike the gong at your convenience and eat." children.translated_text: one should say: "Venerable ones, the forest-dwellers are coming — put in the rice!" But if they do not come by the end of the [proper] time, the village-dwellers should strike the gong and eat. The forest-dwellers' pot should be taken down, washed, and placed in its spot. For sometimes the forest-dwellers may face danger from thieves, danger from water, danger from lions, or danger from tigers, such that they do not come. If some <s>upāsaka</s> (lay follower) invites the <s>Saṃgha</s> to a meal and says: "Venerable ones, inform the forest-dwellers too," then the village-dwellers should also inform the forest-dwellers: "Venerable one, tomorrow there will be a meal, or a before-meal, or a gruel-drinking; do not go on alms-round; come early in the morning." And the forest-dwellers should not disregard [this]. If they want [the food], they should wait. They should come at the proper time. If [the food] is not ready, one should not sit occupying the meal-hall. Rather, having worshipped the <s>cetiya</s>, one should study privately to one side, or sit contemplating the <s>Dharma</s>. Now if someone invites the village-dwellers to a meal, one should say: "Invite the forest-dwellers too." But if [the inviter] says: "I have no faith or confidence in them," one should say: "Then we too will not accept." But if he invites the forest-dwellers too, the food should be prepared, water strained, and seats arranged. When the donor has arrived but the forest-dwellers have not come, and the donor says: "Venerable sirs, strike the gong — the time is passing," one should say: "Wait — the forest-dwellers have not yet come." But if the donor says: "Venerable sirs, strike [the gong] — the forest-dwellers will come eventually" — what should be done? The gong should be struck at length, the <s>cetiya</s> worshipped at length. After worshipping the <s>cetiya</s> at length, if the forest-dwellers have arrived, then one should eat. But if the forest-dwellers have not arrived, leaving empty seats for those next [in line], one should sit down. The server should be asked: "Who is the share-collector for the forest-dwellers?" If they say: "I am! I am!" one should say: "Set aside the forest-dwellers' alms-food." The forest-dwellers' alms-food should be set aside and placed in the <s>Saṃgha</s>'s preparation-hut. If they arrive at the proper time, it should be given for eating. But if they arrive at the wrong time, or do not come, the next day it should be given to the <s>śrāmaṇeras</s> (novices). And it is not proper for the forest-dwellers to sit in idle neglect. Rather, from time to time they should go to the village lodging. Having arrived, washed feet, cleaned hands, and worshipped the <s>cetiya</s> at length — if there is still time, one should dwell engaged in the practice of standing, walking, sitting, and <s>yoga</s>, or engaged in recitation or mindfulness. When it is mealtime, one should enter the monastery grounds, greet the village-dwelling <s>bhikṣus</s>, and sit at one's own seat. When the gong has been struck and the <s>cetiya</s> worshipped, the forest-dwellers should not disparage the village-dwellers: "You busy-bodies with much to do! You seek flavors on the tip of the tongue!" Rather, they should be honored, saying: "Venerable ones, well done! You bear the burden of much work. You give <s>Dharma</s> teachings. The monastery is beautified. Smoke rises [from cooking]. The lay families are inspired." Thus

children.translated_text: [one should] sit attending [to the matter]: 'Are the village-adjacent [monks] coming?' 'No.' If they do come, rice should be added for them too. But if they do not come, at the proper time, having struck the bell and worshipped the shrine, one should eat. For the village-adjacent monks, their bowls should be set down and the bowls should be rinsed with water and stored. Now if someone invites the forest-dwelling monks to a meal, one should say: 'Invite the village-adjacent monks also.' But if they say: 'I have no faith in them, no confidence,' one should say: 'Then we too do not accept [your invitation].' But if he also invites the village-adjacent monks, the meal should be prepared; the seating arrangement should be made; the drinking water should be strained; flowers should be prepared; incense should be prepared. If the village-adjacent monks have not yet come and the donor arrives and says: 'Venerable ones, strike the bell — it is still the proper time,' one should say: 'It is still early; the village-adjacent monks have not yet come.' But if he says: 'Strike [the bell]; the village-adjacent ones will also come,' what should be done? The bell should be struck at length. The shrines should be worshipped at length. Having worshipped the shrines at length, if the village-adjacent monks have arrived, one should eat. But if the village-adjacent monks

children.translated_text: The server should ask: 'Who receives the alms-portions for the village-adjacent monks?' If they say: 'I do, I do,' he should say: 'Then receive the alms-food for the village-adjacent monks.' But if there is no one to receive [their portions], the server should gather together the alms-food of all into one place and store it in the <s>saṃgha</s>'s allowable-food hut. If they come at the proper time, [the food] should be given [to them] to eat. But if they arrive after the proper time, or do not come at all, the next morning it should be given to the novices or the monastery attendants. Nor is it proper for the village-adjacent monks to sit fixated [on the forest-dwellers' food]. Rather, from time to time they should go to the forest-dwelling quarters, wash the feet, clean the hands, and worship the <s>stūpa</s> at length. If it is the proper time, they should pass the time in gardens, at the bases of trees, on walkways, and in sitting-places, devoted to the practice of standing, walking, and sitting meditation — engaged in recitation or in mental cultivation. Then at the proper time, having entered the dwelling, having exchanged greetings with the forest-dwelling monks, each should sit in his own seat. When the bell has been struck, having worshipped the <s>stūpa</s>, having eaten, one should go. Nor should the village-adjacent monks revile or insult the forest-dwellers: 'You dwellers of empty houses! You, the wise and clever ones! Even jackals live in the forest! All day long you just sit collecting rains [years]!' Rather, they should be told: 'Difficult to dwell in are the forest-dwelling quarters — remote, secluded, far from inhabited areas, suited for solitary retreat, bereft of human company, conducive to meditative seclusion. Difficult is solitude; difficult is delight in being alone. The mind spending even one more night [there] goes inward.' 'Venerable ones, a fine thing is being done! The forest-dwelling quarter is being maintained!' And the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'As long as you monks will dwell in forest-dwelling quarters, only growth is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not decline. And <s>Māra</s>, the Evil One, will not find an opportunity for the disappearance and confusion of the True <s>Dharma</s>.' Having thus encouraged [them], one should go. Thus should the forest-dwellers conduct themselves. If they do not so conduct themselves, they transgress the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). //*//

V.1-2 Ms.30b5 (J.140.1); Ch.509c26 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s>, the Perfectly Awakened One (<s>samyaksaṃbuddha</s>), having accomplished the purpose for which he arose, was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: Now there were forest dwellings and village-adjacent [dwellings], with a single-meal arrangement. At the village-adjacent dwelling, [this arrangement] benefited both the forest-dwellers and the village-adjacent [monks]. By those village-adjacent [monks], as a matter of course, the bell should be struck and [they should] stand ready. Those forest-dwellers, [arriving] at the proper time, came to the village-adjacent dwelling.

Into those vessels should be put <s>pāṭalā</s> (trumpet-flower) pills, or <s>campaka</s> (champak) pills, or sugar — whatever should be done so that [the water] becomes fragrant. Then, if there is separate water for drinking and separate [water] for foot-washing, [both] should be strained. With the foot-washing water, the <s>śirikuṇḍikā</s> (water-vessel) should be filled; the non-allowable jug should be filled; the foot-washing basin should be filled; the privy-jar should be filled. For the monks, the vessels and pots for hand-water, bowl-water, and personal-use [water] should be filled. There are established [water sources in different cities]: in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s>, the <s>Śoṇa</s> water; in <s>Rājagṛha</s>, hot-spring [water]; in <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, the lotus-pool called <s>Buddhavicīrṇā</s>; in <s>Campā</s>, <s>Gaṅgā</s> water; in <s>Śrāvastī</s>, [the spring] <s>Potaleya</s>; in <s>Sāketa</s>, <s>Dhara</s> water; in <s>Mathurā</s>, the <s>Yamunā</s>. children.translated_text: should be given. But if the <s>bhikṣu</s> is faithful, he may fill the <s>śrīkuṇḍikā</s> (sacred water-pot) from there — no offence. If a <s>bhikṣu</s>'s eyes are aching and a physician says: 'Venerable sir, wash your eyes with fresh water' — he may then take a bowl-full. Now this [<s>bhikṣu</s>] does washing or dyeing [with the water]. If he needs water, he requests from the water-distributor: 'I want water to be given.' It is not proper to give fresh water. Rather, rinsing-water should be given. When distributing water before the meal, having thoroughly cleaned the hands, having thoroughly cleaned the vessel, clean water should be distributed. When taking water, one should hold [the vessel] firmly so that one hand remains free of food residue. But if through haste it has become soiled, having washed [it] with a leaf-branch or bowl, if the lip [of the vessel] is slippery, having wiped it clean, one should drink. One should not put too much lip [on the vessel], or let hair touch it, or the forehead. Rather, having wiped the lip, one should drink from the tip of the lips. Just that little bit should be left aside. Having rinsed with that same end, it should be discarded. When distributing water, one should observe: if anyone puts too much lip [in the water], or if hair falls in, or [it touches] the forehead, that vessel should be removed, set aside to one side, and grass or a twig placed on top as a sign that it is unfit for use. Or it should be cleaned again. When distributing water after the meal, having thoroughly cleaned the hands — abbreviated — up to: with one hand the water should be held, with the other, when receiving the water-pot, it should be held with the robe-end or the bowl-edge, up to: with that same edge

children.translated_text: should be secured. When drinking, the lips should be cleaned with a leaf-branch, and one should drink from the tip of the lips — abbreviated — the same should be done. When serving in the meditation hall, if there is floor-covering, the vessels should be placed on leaf-branches, or on sand, or on [other] vessels. If those seated [fill] an eighth or a quarter [of the hall], one person standing in the middle should serve, another should pass [the water]. But if [the monks] are seated far apart in order, far from the meditation hall, one should serve — abbreviated. It is allowed to wash the face or clean the hands or wash the bowl-strainer with rinsing-water. It is not proper to discard [water] by splashing carelessly. It should be brought close in measured amounts. It is not proper to bathe with rinsing-water, or to wash robes, or to extract dye. But if the <s>bhikṣus</s> are doing robe-work and the water is muddy and the vessel has surplus, it is allowed to request from a subordinate monk, saying: 'Venerable one, give [this]; I will bring more and return it.' Even if he gives, no offence. Having taken it, he should bring and return it from time to time. But if the monastery is near a water source, even if one drinks from there, makes rinsing-water from there, washes hands from there, or makes dye from there — no offence. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding water. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

V.3-4 Ms. 32b2 (J.147.13); Ch. 508b22 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. At that time, the venerable <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s> were guarding the drinking water. Those monks washed their faces and cleaned their hands from that same [water]. They washed their bowl-strainers [in it]. Now <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>, having risen early in the morning, having washed their hands, having strained the drinking water, having locked up the water-pavilion and sealed it, went out for the alms-round. Visiting monks arrived and searched for drinking water but could not find any. They then complained: 'Why has this water-pavilion been locked and sealed?' The monks heard of this matter and reported it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, monks, <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>...' in abbreviated form, up to: '...visiting monks, a whole group, arrived, searched for drinking water, and could not find any. They then complained: "Why has this water-pavilion been locked and sealed?"' They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus regarding drinking water. One should conduct oneself thus regarding foot-washing water. And how should one conduct oneself regarding drinking water and foot-washing water? It is not proper, having strained the drinking water, to lock and seal the water-pavilion and go elsewhere. Rather, a water-attendant should be appointed — from the junior end, or in rotation, or whoever is available. One, or two, or three, or as many as can manage. By them, having risen early in the morning and washed the hands, the drinking water should be strained. [Vessels such as] round pots, or small jars, or pitcher-vessels, or stoppered jars, or long-necked flasks, or wide-mouthed jars, or water-pots should be covered. They should be bound with stone, clay, or wooden [covers], or with clean cloth-strips, making them well-secured and stored.

children.translated_text: <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Upanandana</s>, and the <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s> (Group of Six monks), at the foot-washing place, having splashed and washed their feet, spilled all the water, overturned the foot-washing vessel, and with wet feet thrust [them] into their sandals, not avoiding either mud or dust, trampling through mud and dust, walked back and forth on a long walking-meditation path. [Other] <s>bhikṣus</s> came to wash their feet. They then said: 'Venerable ones, wash your feet in moderation! Even regarding water, moderation has been declared by the <s>Bhagavān</s>, and likewise regarding all external requisites of life.' Those <s>bhikṣus</s> saw the foot-washing vessel empty and overturned. They then grumbled: 'Why has this foot-washing vessel been overturned?' The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Upanandana</s>, and the <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s>.' They were summoned.

'Speak in moderation. Venerable ones, wash your feet — with water too the <s>Bhagavān</s> has spoken of moderation.' Likewise with all the requisites of life. The monks then saw that the foot-washing basin had been placed upside down. They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'You have done wrong, <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Upanandana</s>, and the group-of-six. Therefore, thus should the feet be washed. And thus should one conduct oneself after washing the feet. How then should the feet be washed? How should one conduct oneself after washing the feet?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> then addressed the monks:
'Monks, wash your feet as the elder <s>Śāriputra</s> does. At one time, the elder <s>Śāriputra</s> was dwelling at <s>Vaiśālī</s>, in the Great Forest, at the Gabled Hall. The elder, having dressed early in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered the city of <s>Vaiśālī</s> for alms — with graceful going and returning, with [proper] looking ahead and looking aside, with [proper] bending and stretching, with [proper] wearing of the <s>saṃghāṭī</s> (triple robe), bowl, and robes, with senses restrained, with mind not outward-directed, steady, abiding in the natural state of <s>Dharma</s>, mindful and clearly comprehending, as if guided along a marked path, he walked for alms in the city of <s>Vaiśālī</s>. The elder was then seen by a certain <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. That <s>brāhmaṇa</s> thought: "These are sons of slaves — petty ascetics who practice deportment at the edge of the village — they are washed out and they deteriorate." So with hostile intent, he followed behind the elder, [thinking:] "Wherever this ascetic deteriorates in deportment, right there I will give him a smack on the head." The elder, endowed with the same deportment in village and forest alike, having walked for alms in <s>Vaiśālī</s> and having returned to the monastery, set down his bowl in the dwelling, washed his hands, beat out and folded his <s>saṃghāṭī</s>, doubled it up on the inside, and placed it on the robe-rack. Having filled a basin with drinking water, prepared a stool, brought out a foot-scraper, brought out the sandal-cloth and sandals, he washed his feet. The elder poured water with his right hand and washed his feet with his left hand. The elder washed the left calf, washed the right calf, washed the left foot, washed the right foot. Taking the sandal-wiping cloth, he put the sandals together as a pair, wiped the strap of one sandal, wiped the strap of the second sandal, wiped the sole of one sandal, wiped the sole of the second sandal. Having set down the sandal-cloth, from the basin he poured water with the left water-pot, washed the sandal-wiping cloth with his right hand, wrung it out, and set it in the sun to dry. Pouring water from the water-pot, he washed his hands, washed his hands, washed the basin, discarded the remaining water, and set [the basin] in the sun to dry. That <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, seeing his meticulous conduct, was delighted. With a pleased mind he said: "Just as this basin has been handled by the venerable <s>Śāriputra</s> — even the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>' hot-water pot is not kept this clean. Indeed, one could drink water from this!" The elder then taught that <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, whose mind was pleased, the Four Noble Truths (<s>catvāri āryasatyāni</s>): the Noble Truth of suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), the Noble Truth of the origin of suffering (<s>duḥkhasamudaya</s>), the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering (<s>duḥkhanirodha</s>), and the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (<s>duḥkhanirodhagāminī pratipad</s>). That <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, standing right there on that spot, directly realized the fruit of stream-entry (<s>śrotāpattiphala</s>). The monks then said to the <s>Bhagavān</s>: 'Whose [merit is this], <s>Bhagavān</s>, that this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> was pleased by the elder's meticulous conduct?' The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Not only now [was he pleased] — in the past too this one was pleased by his meticulous conduct.' 'In the past too, <s>Bhagavān</s>?' 'In the past, monks — in a former time, in a past age, there was this city of <s>Vārāṇasī</s> in the <s>Kāśi</s> country. There lived a leading householder, wealthy, of great riches, great possessions, with abundant stores of wealth, grain, treasuries, and granaries, with abundant gold, silver, money, and equipment, with abundant elephants, horses, goats, and sheep, with abundant female and male servants, workers, and employees. He had one son, recently born. He was raised and brought up by his mother and father. When he was seven or eight years old, he would rise before his parents, go to sleep after them, speak pleasantly, and not speak offensively — a willing servant. Now some rogues frequented that merchant's house. His house was well-guarded and well-protected; they could not find an opening [to rob it]. Then one time, that merchant was invited to a relative's hall for a rainy-season night. Placing that boy as a guard — "Son, fasten the door and sit guarding." That boy, with the merchant and his retinue having left, sat guarding with the door fastened. Those rogues then found their opening. They entered the house by climbing over. Having lit torches and lamps, they searched. One boy was found. They then asked: "Boy, where is your family's silver and gold?" He said: "I too do not know. This house is empty — search and search, and whatever you find, take it." They then searched and searched, and [finding] abundant gold and silver, made a great heap in the center of the house. Their thief-chief sat in the central room. That thief-chief became thirsty. He said to the boy: "Come now, boy, I am thirsty; I wish to drink water." That boy, accustomed to meticulous conduct, took a vessel, wiped it clean, washed his hands thoroughly, washed the vessel thoroughly, filled it with water, and where the lamp was burning, there he positioned himself. Having carefully examined [the water], he offered it to the thief-chief — "Drink, chief." By that thief-chief too, the boy's entire manner of serving the water was observed. He then asked: "Come now, boy, for what reason have you positioned yourself here at the lamplight?" He said: "Chief, to examine the water, lest there be a blade of grass or an insect in the water, and the chief would be

It is not proper to put on the sandals with wet feet. Rather, when [the feet] are thoroughly dry, then [the sandals] should be put on. Now if there is a communal foot-washing facility for the entire <s>Saṃgha</s>, it is not proper for a <s>bhikṣu</s> to wash his feet with splashing, spilling water, [or] making the foot-washing facility overflow. Rather, snapping the fingers [to announce oneself], one should approach the foot-washing facility. If some <s>bhikṣu</s> has entered earlier, one should wait until he has washed his feet. Rather, when the feet have been washed, one should rise and go, avoiding the dust. And it is not proper, after the feet have been washed, to walk back and forth on a long walking-path. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s> is doing his recitation and walks about after having washed his feet, they should be washed again. But if it is wintertime and the <s>bhikṣu</s> thinks: "Who will wash [them] again?" — at the very least, having wiped [them] with a cloth-strip or with the left hand, one should enter. Thus should feet be washed. Thus should one conduct oneself after washing the feet. One who does not so conduct himself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). ////

The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "<s>Bhikṣus</s>, you might think thus: 'That was another person at that time and on that occasion' — the son of a leading family. It should not be viewed thus. That was the elder <s>Śāriputra</s>; the other was the thief-commander; this was the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. Then too, he was pleased by this one's sphere of good conduct; now too, he is pleased by the elder's sphere of good conduct." Now when this <s>bhikṣu</s> has gone out from the village, then the village-entry robe should be shaken out, the utmost grooming completed, and [the robe] set aside. The monastery-robe should be put on, the seat arranged, a foot-rest [set], water-vessel set up, dust wiped off with a cloth-strip, the water-basin tilted, the cloth washed, wrung out, and the sandals cleaned — and so on — up to: the cloth wrung out and set aside, lest insects arise or mold develop. And when a <s>bhikṣu</s> is washing his feet, he should pour water with the right hand and wash the feet with the left hand. First the left shin should be washed, then the right shin; the left foot should be washed, then the right foot. The sandals should be shaken out, paired together, and the strap of one sandal

children.translated_text: 'Venerable ones, open the door!' They said: 'Wait, venerable ones; the bathhouse is not yet hot.' When the monks had assembled, at that time [the group-of-six] used up all the oil, used up all the powder, poured away all the water, threw all the firewood into the fire, locked the bathhouse, and ran out. They said: 'Enter, venerable ones — the bathhouse is heated!' Those monks, stricken by the cold, rushed in hastily. At that time, those venerable group-of-six monks had latched the door and barricaded it from outside. Those [monks inside] searched for oil — could not find any; searched for powder — could not find any. Tormented by heat and smoke, they could not find water. They came to the door — but it had been barricaded from outside. They said: 'Venerable group-of-six monks! Move aside from the door! We are dying from smoke and heat!' A furnace should be made — wide at the bottom of the doorway, narrow at the top. The chimney [height], measured by fist-lengths, should be three cubits. The fire-pit, measured by fist-lengths in width, should be made from the ground up, half a cubit thick. A fire-flue should be made. [The space] around the furnace should all be [enclosed]. A door-panel should be made. If the furnace is on the right side, the door-panel should be made on the left. But if the furnace is on the left, the door-panel should be made on the right. It is not proper to make a needle-bolt [fastener]; a latch-bolt should be made. Nor should it be made [too hot], such that it is comfortable to heat. Rather, it should be made so that it is just hot enough to produce results. Outside, a robe-hut should be made. Elephant-tusk hooks should be made — serving this very purpose. children.translated_text: has been struck, one should know: is this bathhouse for the whole <s>saṃgha</s>, for a particular precinct, or for a group? If it is for a group, those who belong to that group should go there. But if it is for a particular precinct, those who belong to that precinct should go. But if it is for the whole <s>saṃgha</s>, then when bathing, one should gather one's robes and place them in one spot — on a canvas, or a cloth, or a robe-rack, or a bathhouse stool. When entering, it is not proper to enter swinging the arms. Rather, one should enter with one hand covering the front. When one [monk] is going out and another is entering, the one entering should give way. It is not proper to step over seats, or vessels, or a senior monk when going. One should go mindfully. Now if the preceptor or teacher has entered [the bathhouse], one should not call out from outside: 'I am bathing, teacher! I am bathing, preceptor!' Rather, having set aside one's robes and entered, one should first attend to him. But if one wishes to attend to another also, one should ask permission first. But if he has been previously instructed: 'You should attend to so-and-so or so-and-so,' then even if one does so without asking, there is no offence. If the fire is intense, the juniors should stand in front, shielding [the elders] from the fire. But if the fire is low, the elders should stand in front.
