children.translated_text: or a cloth strip should be given. But if the donors say: 'Let the venerable ones bring as much as they need' — even so, only a moderate amount should be brought. When entering the bathhouse, one should know the conditions of water: how is it provided? If it is given in measured amounts, the hot water should be received in a pot or basin, and thus taken accordingly. But if they naturally say: 'Whoever is able to prepare the water, let him enter' — whoever is able to prepare the water should enter. But if the pupils or co-residents say: 'Preceptors and teachers, enter; we will prepare the water' — one should enter, and even so, only a moderate amount should be used. Or if lay followers, workers, or monastery attendants say: 'Enter, venerable assembly; we will provide the water' — one should enter, using only a moderate amount. But if there is a river, a lotus-pond, or a lake, even if they bring as much as needed — no offence. It is not proper in the open to perform bathing services naked to a naked [person]. But if the water provides cover, or if the water is navel-deep — no offence. But if the water is only knee-deep, one should do [the bathing] while seated, so that the navel area is covered. It is not proper to take one's own robes and mix them up with another's robes and leave them. Rather, having placed them in their proper spot, one should go. When the bathhouse has been announced, one should know: is this bathhouse for the entire <s>Saṃgha</s>, for an assembly, for a precinct, or for those invited? According to how it is, one should go. If it is for the entire <s>Saṃgha</s>, the whole <s>Saṃgha</s> should go. If it is for an assembly, those [of that assembly] should go. If it is for a precinct, those of the precinct should go. If it is for those invited, those invited should go. But if it is announced: 'Venerable ones, those who have oil and powder, let them come' — then those who have oil and powder should go. But if the <s>bhikṣus</s> are weakened by old age or weakened by illness,

children.translated_text: it should be said: 'Preceptors and teachers, come bathe; we will apply the oil.' If one wishes to bathe, one should go. But if one does not wish to bathe, one should say: 'Fellow monks of the same lineage, go yourselves; I will not bathe.' But if the bathhouse belongs to the <s>Saṃgha</s>, or if the lay donors provide [supplies], the bell should be struck and an announcement made: 'Venerable ones, there will be oil, there will be powder, there will be water — let the venerable ones bathe.' The bathhouse attendants should be requested. By them the bathhouse should be heated, the bathhouse seats brought in, the oil brought in, the powder brought in, the shells brought in, the water heated. If the oil and powder are scarce, measured amounts should be given. The oil should be conserved, the water [supply] maintained. But if there is abundance, the <s>Saṃgha</s> steward announces or says: 'Bathe confidently, venerable ones.' Even so, the proper measure of oil should be known. The junior <s>bhikṣus</s> should perform body-care for the senior <s>bhikṣus</s>. It is not proper for the junior <s>bhikṣus</s> to bathe with loud splashing. Rather, they should bathe with mutual respect, with proper restraint. It is not proper to bathe with loud sounds and great noise. Rather, one should bathe in the bathhouse with soft sounds and little noise. But if a [doctrinal] question is posed, even if they answer in a resounding voice — no offence. When the <s>bhikṣus</s> have finished bathing, the bathhouse attendant should store any remaining oil, store any remaining powder, wash and store the bathhouse seats, wash and store the shells. Whatever firewood remains should be placed in its proper location. But if someone enters afterward: 'Come, venerable ones; we will store these things' — one should go, and they should store [the items]. Let no danger arise. Having sprinkled and swept the bathhouse, having removed the embers, having closed up the bathhouse, one should go. Thus

children.translated_text: If this <s>Saṃgha</s> has a regular benefaction, a permanent cook should be appointed, or a monthly attendant, or a ten-day attendant, or a five-day attendant. By him the <s>Saṃgha</s>'s benefaction should be arranged and the <s>bhikṣu-saṃgha</s> should be served. When the <s>bhikṣu-saṃgha</s> has eaten, whatever utensils are there — iron [vessels], basins, cooking pots, or small stools — by the monthly or fortnightly attendants, having summoned the kitchen-servant, having them cleaned and greased, they should be placed upside down facing the sun. When they are dry, they should be brought into the preparation-hut and placed in their proper location. Whatever is there — milk-pots, yogurt-pots, or sauce-containers — they should be well-washed, well-rinsed, and placed in the sun. When they are dry, they should be brought into the preparation-hut and stored. Whatever is there — copper strainers, copper vessels, iron vessels, ladles, spatulas, cups, bowls, or plates — they should be cleaned, brought into the preparation-hut, and placed in their proper location.

children.translated_text: the elder's [need] should be ascertained. But if the elder's [task] takes a long time and the junior's [task] is for a short time, the junior should be given [priority]. But if for both it is for a short time, the elder should be given [priority]. If for both it takes a long time, the elder should be given [priority]. Having done the washing or dyeing, it is not proper to return [the equipment] as-is — soiled, dye-stained, unwashed, or unsmeared. Rather, having well-washed, well-cleaned, well-smeared, and well-dried [it] — the robe-line: after dyeing robes, one should not leave the awning just as it is and go. Rather, having gathered [it], it should be stored in its proper place. There are carpenter's tools: an adze, a saw, a chisel, or a plumb-line — having washed, they should be stored to one side. There are craftsman's tools: an axe, an adze, a scraper, a hammer, or a bolt — they should be stored to one side. These are: adzes, spades, or ladders — they should not be stored just as they are, smeared with mud. Rather, having washed them, they should be stored in their proper place. Now this communal <s>Saṃgha</s> property belonging to [monks from] the four directions — when not in use, after use, it should not be hidden and stored away in the dwelling. It will be convenient for future use. Rather, whoever has need of it, to him it should be given. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding equipment. One who does not practice thus transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

V.9 Ms.38a1 (J.171.3); Ch.509b14 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background of five reasons in detail, up to: the <s>Bhagavān</s> saw, on his five-day tour of the monastery dwellings, walking about and inspecting — the utensils in the monastery dwellings were abandoned and strewn about: cooking pots, small stools, unwashed and ungreased, being gnawed by rats and mice; rice-cooking vessels [with] handles being pecked at by crows and birds; troughs, ladles, bowls, food-tables, water-pots, baskets, spoons, and trays. The <s>Bhagavān</s>, knowing, asked: 'Why, <s>bhikṣus</s>, are these utensils lying about abandoned and strewn?'

children.translated_text: matter the monks reported to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon that monk.' He was summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'So you, monk, grabbed the robe by the corner and pulled, and it tore completely. Therefore, thus should one conduct oneself regarding robes. And how should one conduct oneself regarding robes? When many monks sleep in a single dwelling — if that dwelling is overcrowded — it is not proper for monks to place their robes loosely. Rather, the robes should be gathered up, folded double with the inside facing in, and placed on the robe-pole. Then, with a band, a cord, or a rope, they should be tied. The <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor)'s or <s>ācārya</s> (teacher)'s robe, having been gathered, should be placed first, folded with care, at the front. When pressed for space, one should not wrap one's own robe with the <s>upādhyāya</s>'s or <s>ācārya</s>'s robes. Rather, with one's own robes, the <s>upādhyāya</s>'s and <s>ācārya</s>'s robes should be wrapped [for protection]. Thus, all [robes] should be tied and stored. children.translated_text: [the robes]. Now if the dwelling is dusty, it is not proper to place the preceptor's (<s>upādhyāya</s>) or teacher's (<s>ācārya</s>) robes on top and one's own robes below. Rather, the preceptor's or teacher's [robes] should be placed below, and one's own robes on top. Nor is it proper — when it is summer and dust or wind-blown dust or moths destroy the robes — to wrap one's own robes with the preceptor's or teacher's robes. Rather, one's own robes should be used to wrap the preceptor's or teacher's robes. Nor should the dwelling be neglected, [whether it is] dusty or unclean. Rather, from time to time it should be sprinkled and swept. Cow-dung plaster should be applied. Drains should be provided. It is not proper to handle the robe with dirty [hands] — or to use [the robe] to handle a spittoon, a feces-basin, a urinal, refuse, or to take [off] sandals, or to collect cow-dung. Nor should the robe be neglected — [whether it is] greasy, unrepaired, soiled, dirty, or torn and ripped. Rather, from time to time it should be washed, dyed, and sewn. As one [cares for] one's skin, so should one conduct oneself regarding the robe. One who does not so conduct himself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

V.10 Ms. 38b6 (J.175.3); Ch. 509c9 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: In one dwelling, many monks were sleeping. Now that dwelling was overcrowded. Another monk, during the night, needing to relieve himself, went out. His robe, pulled from the robe-pole, fell. Thus it fell to the ground. It was then trodden on by one, trodden on by a second, trodden on by a third — completely soiled with mud. Only a corner of the robe remained. children.translated_text: when entering — it is not proper to set aside the village-entering lower robe without having it ready at hand, and [then] cast off the monastery-wear lower robe. Rather, as a matter of course, the village-entering lower robe should first be made ready at hand. Then the village-entering lower robe should be wrapped around, and the monastery-wear lower robe should be lifted up. Having fastened the waist-band and having put on the upper robe, one should enter for alms. Having returned from the alms-round, it is not proper to set aside the monastery-wear lower robe without having it ready at hand, and [then] cast off the village-entering lower robe. Rather, as a matter of course, the monastery-wear lower robe should first be made ready at hand. Then the monastery-wear lower robe should be wrapped around, and the village-entering lower robe should be lifted up. If the monks wish to do cleaning work — plastering or sweeping — and wish to bathe wearing a bathing cloth or a cloth strip, it is not proper to cast off the lower robe and put on a bathing cloth or cloth strip. Rather, the lower robe should be lifted up, and the bathing cloth or cloth strip should be wrapped around, with the lower robe lifted up. Nor is it proper while bathing, having put on the lower robe, to remove the bathing cloth from above the lower robe like a pleasure-seeker.

VI.2 Ms.40a3 (J.181.7); Ch.511b27 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable group-of-six (<s>ṣaḍvargika</s>) [monks], setting out for the alms-round, would set aside their monastery-wear upper robes and, with only a single lower garment, search for their village-entering upper robes. Having returned from the alms-round, they would set aside their village-entering upper robes and, with only a single lower garment, search for their monastery-wear upper robes. The monks heard this matter. The monks reported [it] to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Summon the group-of-six.' They were summoned. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Is it true, monks, group-of-six, that thus you set out early for the alms-round, set aside your monastery-wear upper robes, and with only a single lower garment search for your village-entering upper robes; and having returned from the alms-round, you set aside your village-entering upper robes and with only a single lower garment search for your monastery-wear upper robes?' They said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should one put on the upper robe. And how should one put on the upper robe? When a monk sets out early in the morning for the alms-round, it is not proper to set aside the monastery-wear upper robe and, with only a single lower garment, search for the village-entering upper robe. Rather, as a matter of course, the village-entering upper robe should first be made ready at hand. When putting on the upper robe, the village-entering upper robe should be wrapped around, and the monastery-wear upper robe should be lifted up. Having come out from the alms-round, it is not proper to set aside the village-entering upper robe and, with only a single lower garment, search for the monastery-wear upper robe. Rather, as a matter of course, the monastery-wear upper robe should first be made ready at hand. When putting on [the upper robe], the monastery-wear upper robe should be wrapped around, and the village-entering upper robe should be lifted up. Thus

children.translated_text: And how should one conduct oneself regarding robes when entering the inner quarters? It is not proper for a <s>bhikṣu</s> entering the inner quarters to enter dragging the robe — wherever it gets caught, there it gets caught; wherever it tears, there it tears. Rather, if it is the hot season and the village is far away, the robe should be placed on the head or shoulder and one should go. When one reaches the village border, if there is a stream, a pond, or a lotus-pool, there one should wash the feet, put on the robe, tie the knot-side, and enter. But if there is no water, with a leaf-branch or grass the feet and shins should be wiped, then the robe should be put on and one should enter. But if it is winter, the robe should be worn while going. With the robe evenly wrapped, one should enter the inner quarters, avoiding: a runaway horse, a runaway elephant, a runaway chariot-horse, a mare, an ox-and-cart — and avoiding thorn-branches, and avoiding white-plastered walls,

VI. 3 Ms.40b2 (J.183.1); Ch. 511c7 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>, when entering [households] for alms, entered dragging their robes — [robes would] get caught on thorn-branches; they would rip and tear. When caught on a bush or tree-branch, they would rip and pull. They did not avoid dust, nor did they avoid mud. In narrow streets they went rubbing against white-plastered walls. Their robes became tangled, torn, and ripped. Their co-residents and pupils complained: "We go about washing, sewing, and dyeing robes until we are exhausted, yet they do not even know how robes should be handled when entering the inner quarters." The <s>bhikṣus</s> heard this matter and reported it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Summon <s>Nandana</s> and <s>Upanandana</s>." They were summoned. children.translated_text: You sit rubbing against white-plastered walls, entering and ruining [your] robes. Your co-residents and pupils complain: 'Look at them! We ourselves go about washing, sewing, and dyeing robes until we are exhausted, yet they do not know how robes should be handled after entering the inner quarters.'" They said: "Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>." The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: "Therefore, one should conduct oneself thus regarding robes after entering the inner quarters. And how should one conduct oneself regarding robes after entering the inner quarters? Now this <s>bhikṣu</s> has entered the inner quarters and is offered a seat. The seat should be examined. If the seat is smeared with dust or soiled with mud, or if tangled and dirty coverings have been placed, it is not proper to sit there. If it is a family the <s>bhikṣu</s> trusts, one should say: 'Sister, prepare a seat, lest the robes be ruined.' When a proper seat has been prepared — a cushion, a mat, a cover, or a cloth spread — then one should sit. But if it is a faithless family, or one the <s>bhikṣu</s> does not trust, and there is <s>stūpa</s> or <s>Saṃgha</s> business that depends [on visiting], it is not proper to sit like that. Rather, having shaken [the seat] with a cloth-strip or dust-cloth, one should arrange a border-cloth and sit down. But if even that

children.translated_text: one should sit down. Nor is it proper, when one has entered the inner quarters, to rub against plastered and whitewashed walls while passing. It is not proper to lean against a support or a rest-place that is dirty, stained, clean, or freshly whitewashed. But if the monk is weakened by old age or weakened by illness, he should say: 'Sister, please arrange something on the wall where I may lean.' When a bolster, or a quilt, or a coverlet, or a cushion, or a cloth-strip has been arranged there, then one may lean. But if it is a household without faith, or one that the monk does not trust, at the very least one should place even the waist-cloth on the shoulder [as protection] before leaning. It is not proper, when one has entered the inner quarters, to receive [certain items] with one's robe: ghee-fried food, or oil-fried food, or oily rice-grains — those should not be received [in the robe]. Nor should one receive wet flowers, or small ripe fruits, or a cracked bowl. Nor should one clean one's hands with greasy [material], nor wipe one's lips with wet garlands or oily [cloth]. However, one may take firm fruits in the fold of one's robe — jujubes, or plums, or <s>āmalaka</s> (emblic myrobalan), or <s>hārītakī</s> (terminalia), or rice-grains, or unbroken [items], or dry garlands, or bean-pods. But if, despite the monk's care, the robe is soiled by mud, it should be washed. If it is covered in dust, it should be shaken out. If it is torn or ripped, it should be sewn. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the robe when one has entered the inner quarters. If one does not

They thought: 'The way this one runs hastily with a dry mouth and pale lips, anxiously watching the time — he must have been deceived!' They then mocked him: 'Venerable one, your complexion is truly radiant and glowing! Your lips are nicely moistened! 'And I will do something improper there. Do not tell anyone. I am indeed like a father to you.' The <s>Bhagavān</s> related the entire matter in detail, up to: he then said: 'Venerable one, where have I eaten the food I desired? Thus and thus have I been deceived.' He said: 'Yes, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'
  The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'You have done wrong, <s>Upanandana</s>. Therefore, the leading monk should conduct himself thus, and the attendant monk should conduct himself thus. And how should the leading monk conduct himself, and how should the attendant monk conduct himself? It is not proper for a <s>bhikṣu</s> to take on an attendant monk who is not able to share livelihood for both himself and the other. Rather, one who is able to share livelihood for both himself and the other should take on an attendant monk. If this <s>bhikṣu</s> goes as the attendant of his preceptor or teacher, it is not proper for him to walk far behind, nor is it proper to walk heel-to-heel. Rather, one should walk neither too far nor too close. Nor is it proper for the leading monk to walk stiffly with the neck stretched forward. Rather, one should walk gazing ahead about a yoke's length. In case a mad elephant, a mad horse, a mad chariot, a fierce dog, or a fierce ox should come — if it comes from the right side, one should dodge to the left side; if it comes from the left side, one should dodge to the right side. If [the leading monk] has poor eyesight, or is weakened by old age or illness, the attendant monk should say: 'Preceptor' or 'Teacher, [dodge] to the left' or 'to the right.' But if he cannot see, taking him by the hand, he should be guided to one side or the other. If a <s>bhikṣu</s>'s co-resident or pupil takes on an attendant, if he is able to share livelihood for both himself and the other, it should be allowed. But if he is not able, and has already taken him on, the attendant should be dismissed from time to time. It should be done in such a way that [the attendant] is able to stand for alms-food or go to a monastery.
  Now if the <s>bhikṣu</s> wishes to have bloodletting done — from the arm-vein, finger-vein, or forehead — if he is able to share livelihood with the attendant and himself, he should say: 'Wait, we will eat together and then go [for the procedure].' When the bloodletting has been done, both should eat and then go. But if he is not able, the attendant should be dismissed from time to time, saying: 'Go well. I will come [back].' Or wherever he goes with another, having gone for alms or having gone to the monastery, after eating — it is not proper [to say]: 'He has given [food] for my attendant' — and to show favor by [one's] absence. Rather, whether eaten or not eaten, having given the bowl into another's hand, one should go there. If the vein has not been opened, having given appropriate food to the sick, one should go out together. But if the monastery has distant alms-rounds and the <s>bhikṣu</s>, while seeking his own food, runs out of time — even so one should go. If the one who had bloodletting is coming out and this one is entering, if he sees [him] in an alley, he should turn back right there. If he sees him at the city gate, he should turn back from the city gate. If he sees him on the road, he should turn back from the road. From wherever he sees him, from there he should turn back. But if someone pays homage, he should say: 'So-and-so pays homage.' But if [someone] invites, the attendant should note it. The attendant should announce where they came from: 'So-and-so has invited the preceptor' or 'So-and-so is eating in such-and-such a household.' If the leading monk is not able to dedicate the merit, [and they] say: 'Dedicate the merit' — then the attendant should not say [it himself]. Rather, [the leading monk should be told:] 'Just as you enjoy the foremost seat, foremost water, and foremost alms-food, so too you should dedicate the merit.' The attendant should dedicate accordingly. Thus should the leading monk conduct himself. Thus should the attendant monk conduct himself. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

VI. 5-6 Ms.41b6 (J.188.13); Ch. 512a2 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. The venerable <s>Nandana</s> had a brother named <s>Upanandana</s>. He then said to <s>Nandana</s>'s co-resident pupil: 'Come, venerable one, let us enter the village. I will commit some improper act there — do not tell anyone. After all, I am like an uncle to you.' He then said: 'Be like an uncle! Be like a maternal uncle! But if you commit some improper act there, I will report it.' He [<s>Upanandana</s>] then said: 'You will report it?' He said: 'I will report it.' He [<s>Upanandana</s>] then said: 'Come, I will show you [something].' They then approached great families and were invited: 'Noble one, please take your meal! Have your morning-meal! Eat the snacks! Eat the forest fruits! Do as you please.' But he [<s>Upanandana</s>] did not accept anywhere,

Rather, both portions of alms-food should be brought out. While going, the time should be assessed — if one knows it is possible to manage within the proper time, one should go and offer [the food] to him. But if one sees that the time is pressing, nearly at an end, and it is not possible to manage within the proper time — 'lest both of us go without food' — it should be consumed [on the way]. Nor is it proper — merely because one brings alms-food — [to say:] 'I have been requested as an alms-food bringer' — to do a favor by [going] out of sight. Rather, as a matter of course, a tooth-stick should first be chewed [for him]. The hands should be cleaned. The drinking water should be strained. Having filled the water-pot, two seats should be prepared in the practice hall of the dwelling, and a standing-place should be arranged, and one should sit [waiting]. When [the sick monk] has arrived, having seated [him], they should eat together. But if he says: 'Venerable one, you eat — I have already eaten,' he should be offered [food], saying: 'Fill up the remainder; eat whatever you like.' If he desires, having sat down, whatever he likes, that should be eaten. But if he does not desire, [one should say:] 'Venerable one, you eat — I will not eat.'

children.translated_text: VI.10 Ms.44a7 (J.199.4); Ch. 512b26 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the background in detail: Now those [monks] who were required to serve their dependence-period (<s>niśrayakaraṇīya</s>) were going on the alms-round. Their preceptors and teachers set aside oil [for them], set aside snack-portions [for them], watching [for] the time when they would return, [thinking:] 'Then we will share with them.' But they [the dependents] went further and further away and did not return. Their preceptors and teachers then complained: 'We, for their sake, set aside oil, set aside snack-portions; we know when they will return, [thinking:] "Then we will share." Yet they go further and further away and do not return.' The monks heard of this matter and reported it to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should the alms-round goer conduct himself. And how should the alms-round goer conduct himself? This monk is in his dependence-period. It is not proper, having gone on the alms-round, to go further and further away without returning. Nor should the preceptors and teachers, while eating, stand up [and wait, thinking:] "With these alms-round goers we can put a morsel in the mouth." Rather, [the dependent] should sit within sight. And having stood [begging on] the alms-round, he should go to the preceptor or teacher. If he has obtained [alms], the preceptor or teacher should provide assistance — if there is a little porridge, porridge should be given; oil should be given; snack-portions should be shared. But if the preceptor or teacher also has an alms-food [portion], and this one has come from the alms-round, they should eat together — coarse and fine, one kind and another. But if he comes carrying a full bowl of fine, expensive food and says: "Preceptor, teacher — please eat!" — he should be asked: "Well-provided one, where did you get this?" If he says: "Preceptor, teacher — it was given by such-and-such a servant-girl, or by such-and-such a fierce widow, or by such-and-such a eunuch, or by such-and-such an unmarried woman, or by such-and-such a bad <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> (nun), or by such-and-such a bad female novice" — he should be told: "Well-provided one, this kind of person is not to be accepted from. Do not accept from them again." But if he says: "Preceptor, teacher — I spoke with such-and-such a merchant or caravan-leader, recited the word of the <s>Buddha</s>, and being pleased, he gave me this food" — he should be told: "Well-provided one, create good connections, and do not again [be perceived as having] covetous eyes." But if he says: "Preceptor, teacher — please eat," if it should be eaten, [one should eat it]. But if one does not wish [to eat], he should be told: "Well-provided one, eat it yourself; I will not eat." When permission has been given by the preceptor or teacher, then he may eat. If someone invites [him], if he has need, he should accept. But if, having stood [begging on] the alms-round, he then eats by the bank of a river, or a well, or a lotus-pool, and having cleaned his bowl, comes [back] — there is no offence. Thus should the alms-round goer conduct himself. If he does not so conduct himself, he transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). //*//

children.translated_text: should be lit. When the <s>bhikṣu-saṃgha</s> is seated in <s>prahāṇa</s> (meditation), then the lamp-keeper should tend the lamp, [watching] lest anyone doze off. If someone is dozing, he should snap his fingers to wake him and say: "Venerable one, the lamp is reaching you!" That one should be moved to tend [the lamp] and this one should sit down. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s>'s <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor) or <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) is dozing, it is not proper to overlook [it]. Rather, he too should be alerted by snapping the fingers, and one should say: "Preceptor/teacher, the lamp is reaching you there. Sit down; I will tend [it]." That one should tend [the lamp]. But if the <s>bhikṣu</s> is faithful, he says: "Well done; sit down, I will tend [it]." [The lamp] should be given to him. And it is not proper to tend the lamp with the intention of reproach. Nor should the lamp-tenders feel ill will. Rather, the thought should be generated: "They are removing our hindrances." When the meditation has been comfortably concluded, the lamp should be removed from the meditation hall. It is not proper to extinguish the lamp by slapping, or by blowing, or with a robe-corner. Rather, with a wick-pincher, the wick should be drawn out and removed from the oil and extinguished. But if novice <s>bhikṣus</s> are retiring in the meditation hall, the lamp should not be extinguished in the meditation hall. Rather, the lamps outside in the building corners should be extinguished first. The stairway-corridor lamp and the building-cell lamp should be extinguished. If there are means, all night long a lamp should be lit in both the latrine and the urinal-room. But if there are no means, when the <s>bhikṣus</s> have retired, the latrine lamp should be extinguished first. Having extinguished the latrine lamp, the corridor lamp should be extinguished. children.translated_text: the lamp should be extinguished. One should not extinguish suddenly, without notice. Rather, [one should announce:] "Venerable ones, arrange your beds; I will guard the lamp." First the lamp should be shielded by hand. Then one should say: "Do not [be alarmed], venerable one; I am about to extinguish [it]." It is not proper to extinguish by blowing, or with a robe-corner, or by slapping. If the wick is burnt out, the fire-poker should be pulled out — it is extinguished. The embers should be preserved with husks, chaff, bran, or bran-dust. When in the last watch of the night the meditation gong is struck, the lamp-keepers should first light the stairway-corridor lamp. It is not proper to bring the lamp into the meditation hall suddenly, lest the novice <s>bhikṣus</s> be startled and jump up suddenly. Rather, one should announce: "Venerable ones, the lamp is entering!" — "The lamp enters!" When the meditation has been comfortably concluded, the meditation hall lamp should first be extinguished. children.translated_text: your staff has reached [you]; pass it on.' By him it should be passed on. By this one [the drowsy one], one should sit down. It is not proper with the head covered — abbreviated — up to: rather, with one shoulder bared, having arranged the robe, [the staff] should be taken and passed on. But if many [monks] are drowsy, they should not all be made to stand up like a line of ants. Whoever there is the most junior, to him the staff should be given. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s>'s preceptors or teachers are drowsy, it is not proper to neglect them. Rather, having roused them with a finger-snap, one should say: 'Preceptor/teacher, your staff has reached [you].' Out of respect for the <s>Dharma</s>, he should stand up and take it. It is not proper to give the staff to him [directly]. Rather, one should say: 'Sit down; I will pass it on.' The staff should just be passed on. One should not pass it on seeking a chance to look down [at others]. Rather, it should be passed on while attending to the six sense-bases. If anyone is drowsy, [the staff] should be given to him. One should not harbor resentment against them there. Rather, one should think: 'He is doing a great service for us; he is removing the hindrances.' [So] it should be passed on. But if a faithful <s>bhikṣu</s> says: 'Fellow monk of the same lineage, sit down; I will pass it on' — it should be given [to him]. Thus it should be passed on until the meditation session is comfortably concluded. It is not proper for those <s>bhikṣus</s> who pass the staff to become displeased in mind. Rather, one should generate the thought: 'They are removing the hindrances for me.' Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the staff. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>ṣaḍvārgikas</s> (Group of Six monks), while passing the <s>yaṣṭī</s> (staff) — whenever a <s>bhikṣu</s> dozed, they would quickly strike him in the chest or the feet with the staff. Those <s>bhikṣus</s>, being injured, cried out in pain: "Venerable one, I've been hit! I've been hit!" The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.

children.translated_text: VII.3 Ms.46b2 (J.210.4); Ch.513a24 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Having given the <s>nidāna</s> (narrative occasion) in full: now the <s>bhikṣus</s>, while passing the staff in the meditation hall, suffered from the cold. The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, a ball (<s>geṇḍuka</s>) should be made. When a <s>bhikṣu</s> has a ball made, it should be made of grass, straw, cloth-scraps, or thread — wrapped with cotton, bound around the outside with a knot, and tied with thread. It is not proper to make it too hard, nor is it proper to make it too soft. Rather, it should be made such that when dropped on the ground, it bounces up about a yoke's length. It should be passed: either to the junior end, or in order, or to whomever it reaches. This is the origination of the matter. // * //

children.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s> (Group of Six monks), while passing the ball, wrapped a brick-fragment with a cloth-scrap and used it as a ball. Whoever was drowsy, they quickly struck in the chest with the ball, or hit in the side. Those <s>bhikṣus</s>, being harassed, cried out: 'Venerable ones, I am struck! I am struck!' The <s>bhikṣus</s> reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. It is not proper to pass the ball with hostile intent or malicious intent. Rather, the ball should be passed with a mind of loving-kindness and benevolence. It is not proper for the one [who received] the ball being passed to become displeased in mind. Rather, one should guard the mind [thinking]: 'They are removing the hindrances.' If this <s>bhikṣu</s> is drowsy, it is not proper to quickly strike him with the ball. Rather, having placed the ball down again, he should be roused with a finger-snap, saying: 'Venerable one, your ball has reached [you]; stand up and pass it on.' This one should pass it on, that one should sit down. But if a <s>bhikṣu</s>'s preceptor or teacher is drowsy, he too should not be neglected. Rather, having tossed the ball in front [of him] three times, he should be roused with a finger-snap, saying: 'Preceptor/teacher, your ball has reached [you].' Out of respect for the <s>Dharma</s>, he should stand up and take it. [Then] he should sit down. One should not sit seeking a chance to look down [at others]. Rather, one should sit while attending to the six sense-bases. But if he says: 'Sit down; I will pass it on' — then it should be passed on accordingly. But if a faithful <s>bhikṣu</s> says: 'Fellow monk of the same lineage, sit down; I will pass it on' — it should be given [to him]. Thus it should be passed on until the meditation session is comfortably concluded. It is not proper to neglect the ball when it is torn or split. Rather, from time to time it should be moistened, from time to time it should be washed. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the ball. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

children.translated_text: it is not proper to leave the sitting mat in its assigned place and go. Rather, having folded [the mat] in two as assigned, one should go from there. When the second meditation session's [sitting mat] becomes worn, one should bring down [a new one]. It is not proper, having come to the meditation hall, to grasp the sitting mat corner by corner — 'slap, slap!' — and shake it out. Rather, having unrolled the second end of the gathered sitting mat, it should be spread out. Then one should sit. It is also not proper, when the meditation session is comfortably concluded, to grasp the sitting mat corner by corner — 'slap, slap!' — and shake it out. Rather, mindfully gathering it up, placing it on the shoulder, one should go. It is not proper to neglect the sitting mat when it is soiled or torn. Rather, from time to time it should be washed; from time to time it should be moistened. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding the sitting mat. One who does not so conduct oneself transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

VII.5 Ms.47a7 (J.214.12); Ch.513b8 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable group-of-six (<s>ṣaḍvargika</s>) [monks], seated in the practice hall, having removed their sandals from their seats, grasped one [sandal] by the heel-strap with one hand and the second by the heel-strap with the other hand, and clapped them together — 'clap-clap' — disturbing the meditating (<s>yogācāra</s>) monks with the noise. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should one conduct oneself regarding sandals. And how should one conduct oneself regarding sandals? It is not proper for a monk seated in the practice hall to remove his sandals and, grasping one by the heel-strap with one hand and the second with the other, clap them — "clap-clap." Rather, a monk should, as a matter of course, wipe the sandals at the foot-washing [area] and then go down quietly to the practice hall. If the practice hall has a prepared floor-covering, it is not proper to enter the practice hall wearing sandals. Rather, having removed the sandals at the doorway, having entered, having made an <s>añjali</s> (gesture of respect) to the senior [monks], one should sit down according to seniority. But if a monk sees that many sandals might be chewed by mice, or that monks — knowingly or unknowingly — might take [the wrong ones] and leave, what should be done? Having paired them together, taking [them] with the left hand, having tucked [them under the arm], one should go mindfully. At the sitting-place, the paired sandals should likewise be placed beneath the seat, and having placed them, one should sit in the practice hall. When one has comfortably finished in the practice hall, having stood up, the monk should take the sandals — likewise paired — tucking them under the left arm, and go out mindfully. But if there is no prepared floor-covering, one should enter the practice hall wearing sandals. At the senior [end], having loosened the heel-straps of the sandals, one should make obeisance. Having tucked them, with hands joined in respect, one should go [to one's seat]. Having prepared the sitting-cloth at the assigned spot, having removed the sandals, one should sit cross-legged. When one has comfortably finished in the practice hall,

VII.6 Ms.48a1 (J.217.6); Ch.513b25 —
The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable group-of-six (<s>ṣaḍvargika</s>) [monks], seated in the practice hall, with restless intentions, with sides uncovered, were coughing — 'kha-la kha-la' — disturbing the meditating (<s>yogācāra</s>) monks with the noise. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should one cough. And how should one cough? It is not proper for a monk seated in the practice hall, with restless intentions, with sides uncovered, to cough — "khu-lu khu-lu." Rather, if a monk has a cough coming on, the throat should be massaged with the hand. If one cannot suppress it, one should cough mindfully. But if the cough comes on again and again, one should go outside and cough. Or one should take leave of the practice hall and go. Nor is it proper at a meal-invitation, or at a <s>tarpaṇa</s> gathering, or at a formal meeting, with restless intentions, with sides uncovered, to cough — "kha-kha-kha." If a monk has a cough coming on, one should cough mindfully. But if the cough comes on again and again, the neighbor should be told: "Venerable one, set aside my alms-food for me." Then one should go. Nor is it proper for one seated listening to the <s>Dharma</s>, with restless intentions, with sides uncovered, to cough — "kha." If a monk has a cough coming on, the throat should be massaged. If one cannot suppress it, one should cough mindfully. But if the cough comes on again and again, one should take leave of the <s>Dharma</s>-discourse and go. Nor is it proper, in front of the preceptor or teacher, or in front of senior monks, with restless intentions, with sides uncovered, to cough — "kha-kha-kha." Rather,

children.translated_text: seated in the meditation hall, with mischievous intent, they pierced their noses with a brush. They even rolled a thread and inserted it into the nose. They then sneezed with full throat. They thereby disturbed the <s>yogācāra</s> (meditation-practicing) monks with the noise. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should one sneeze. And how should one sneeze? It is not proper for a monk seated in the meditation hall, with mischievous intent, to pierce the nose with a brush, or to roll a thread and insert it into the nose. Nor is it proper to sneeze with full throat, saying "Ha!" But if a sneeze comes to a monk unintentionally, [the urge] should be dispelled. The area around [the nose] should be rubbed, or the nose should be rubbed. But if he cannot dispel it, he should sneeze mindfully, in such a way that he does not disturb his neighbor — with phlegm or nasal mucus. But if the sneeze comes again and again, having informed those in the meditation hall, he should leave. It is also not proper for a monk seated at a meal or a drink-offering to sneeze with full throat with mischievous intent. But if a sneeze comes to the monk, [the urge] should be dispelled. But if he cannot dispel it, he should sneeze mindfully, in such a way that he does not disturb his neighbor — with phlegm or nasal mucus. But if the sneeze comes to the monk again and again, he should say to his neighbor: 'Venerable one, take over my alms-food,' and then leave. Nor is it proper to sneeze with full throat during the hearing of <s>Dharma</s>. But if

Nor is it proper, at a formal assembly, or in front of the <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor) and <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) or elders, to sneeze with full throat with mischievous intent. But if a sneeze comes to the monk, [the urge] should be dispelled. But if he cannot dispel it, he should go to one side and sneeze. If someone sneezes, one should not say 'Live!' (<s>jīva</s>). Rather, if it is an elder, one should say: 'I salute you' (<s>vandāmi</s>). But if a junior sneezes, one should say: 'May it be announced' (<s>āroceti</s>). Thus should one sneeze. One who does not practice thus transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

children.translated_text: itches, with the pad of the thumb or the palm of the hand, [the itch] should be gently relieved. But if it itches again and again and becomes persistent, having informed those in the meditation hall, he should leave. Nor is it proper for a monk, at a meal or a drink-offering or at a formal assembly, with mischievous intent, to scratch with splinters or stones with a 'scratch-scratch' sound. But if a monk is seated at a meal or a drink-offering and some spot itches — things at hand should be used as appropriate. Even if a monk scratches with a brush, a wooden piece, or a splinter, there is no offence — but one should scratch in such a way that one does not disturb the neighbor with the noise. But if the monk has persistent itching and scratches again and again, the bowl should be given to the neighbor [saying]: 'Venerable one, take over my alms-food.' Then he should leave. It is not proper, in front of the <s>upādhyāya</s> (preceptor), <s>ācārya</s> (teacher), or elders, with mischievous intent, to scratch the body with a 'scratch-scratch' sound. Nor is it proper, having stretched out, to scratch the private parts. But if some spot on the monk's body itches, it should be rubbed with the pad of the thumb or the palm of the hand. But if he cannot dispel it and it itches again and again, he should go to one side and scratch. Thus should one conduct oneself regarding scratching. One who does not practice thus transgresses the rules of proper conduct (<s>abhisamācārika dharma</s>). // * //

VII.9 Ms.49a2 (J. 222.6); Ch. 513c11 — The <s>Bhagavān</s> was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Now the venerable <s>Ṣaḍvargīyas</s> (Group of Six monks), seated in the meditation hall, with mischievous intent, yawned. They cracked their joints, making 'crack-crack' sounds. Making 'grr-grr' sounds like lions or tigers, thus they yawned. They disturbed the <s>yogācāra</s> (meditation-practicing) monks with the noise. The monks reported this matter to the <s>Bhagavān</s>. The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Therefore, thus should one yawn. And how should one yawn? It is not proper for a monk seated in the meditation hall, with mischievous intent, having stretched out, to crack the joints with 'crack-crack' sounds, roaring like a lion or a tiger, and thus to yawn. But if the urge to yawn comes to a monk seated in the meditation hall — one should not yawn while cracking the limbs with 'crack-crack' sounds and opening the mouth. [The urge] should be dispelled. The forehead should be rubbed, or the nose should be rubbed. But if he cannot dispel it, having covered the mouth, he should yawn mindfully. One should act in such a way that one does not disturb the neighbor with the noise. But if the urge to yawn comes to the monk again and again, he should go out and yawn. Or, having informed those in the meditation hall, he should leave. Nor is it proper for one seated in the meditation hall to crack the limbs with 'crack-crack' sounds. And how should one conduct oneself regarding passing wind? It is not proper for a monk, with mischievous intent, to knead porridge or parched grain with white [flour], dry it in the sun, and eat it with white [flour]. Nor is it proper to eat <s>bilva</s> fruits, or <s>madana</s> fruits, or such seasonal fruits, or beans, or sesame-sprout [mixtures]. But if a monk, standing for the alms-round, dependent on others for his livelihood, happens to receive porridge or kneaded parched grain with white [flour], or wind-producing fruits — even if he eats them, there is no offence. It is not proper, while seated in meditation, to pass wind with mischievous intent or with a 'ḍhara-ḍhara' [sound]. But if wind comes upon a monk while seated in the meditation hall, one should not strain the sense-organs [trying to hold it]. But if he has a hemorrhoid condition, he should mindfully lift one buttock, open [a space] with the hand, and pass wind — doing it in such a way that the one next to him is not disturbed by the noise. Furthermore, it is not proper for the one who is more senior to lift the buttock [toward the junior]. Rather, the buttock should be lifted toward the one who is more junior. But if the senior and the junior are crouching in the same spot, it is not proper for the most junior member of the <s>saṃgha</s> to lift the buttock toward the <s>saṃgha</s>-elder. Even if one lifts the buttock toward the more senior — there is no offence. But if the monk is unable to pass wind mindfully, he should run out and pass wind [outside]. But if wind comes upon the monk again and again, he should take leave of the meditation [session] and go. Nor is it proper at the meal-invitation, or the refreshment session, to pass wind with mischievous intent. Rather, one should lift one buttock and pass wind. But if wind comes upon the monk again, he should give his bowl to the one next to him and leave. VII.10 Ms.49b1 (J. 224.9); Ch. 513c26 — The <s>Bhagavān</s>, the Perfectly and Fully Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come forth, was dwelling in <s>Śrāvastī</s>, the Teacher of gods and humans — honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, revered, foremost in gains and fame, a recipient of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicines and requisites for the sick. And yet unattached to these, like a lotus [unsoiled] by water — establishing beings who share in merit in [further] merit, establishing beings who share in [the attainment of] fruits in [further] fruits, establishing beings who share in [spiritual] impressions in [further] impressions, sharing the nectar [of <s>Dharma</s>] abundantly with gods and humans, leading hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings to the nectar [of liberation], lifting them up from the great precipice of the wilderness of beginningless and endless birth, old age, death, and <s>saṃsāra</s>, from the dangerous paths of hell, and establishing them on the safe, level, auspicious, firm, fearless ground of <s>nirvāṇa</s> — having won over [the peoples of] <s>Aṅga</s>, <s>Magadha</s>, <s>Mallī</s>, <s>Vajjī</s>, <s>Kāśī</s>, <s>Kośala</s>, <s>Kuru</s>, <s>Pañcāla</s>, <s>Ceti</s>, <s>Vatsa</s>, <s>Matsya</s>, <s>Śūrasena</s>, <s>Śivi</s>, <s>Daśārṇa</s>, <s>Aśvaka</s>, and <s>Avanti</s> — of proven power in knowledge, self-arisen, [dwelling] in divine abodes, <s>Brahmā</s>-abodes, noble abodes, imperturbable abodes, constant abodes — awakened, in the abodes of the awakened; a conqueror, in the abodes of the conqueror; a knower, in the abodes of the knower; omniscient, in the abodes of the omniscient — having attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind. Furthermore, <s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bhagavāns</s> dwell in whatever abodes they wish. Now the venerable group-of-six monks, with mischievous intent, kneaded porridge-balls and parched grain with white [flour], dried them in the sun, and when they were dry, ate them with the white [flour]. They ate <s>bilva</s> (wood-apple) fruits, they ate <s>svātaka</s> fruits and such seasonal fruits, and they ate beans and sesame-sprout [mixtures]. When the bell for the meditation hall was struck, they went to the meditation hall and sat in the four directions. When the <s>bhikṣu-saṃgha</s> was seated, one passed wind; another went 'ḍhara-ḍhara' [making noises]; another said: 'Well done, venerable one! What is this — an annual ritual? Even for eight hundred [coins] one could not wish for such wind! Oh, what a pleasant sound — it is favorable!' They made those sitting next to them smell their fist: 'Smell it, venerable one! Oh, what a delightful fragrance! Oh, what a wonderful fragrance!' They disturbed the meditating monks with the noise. This
